Side 2 is actual beginning as taped.
This is Gene Ramey, with Stanley Dance.
Gene, I think it's a good idea to begin by saying when and where you were born.
I was born in Austin, Texas, April the 4th, 1913. That spot -- the location, is now Breckenridge Hospital, so I call that a personal monument to myself.
(Laughter.)
This was right near the capital. It was the 600 block, on 13th, in the middle of the block. So it was six blocks from the Austin state capital. It was a very small city then.
How big is it now?
It's a little larger than Kansas City now. 'it's about 300 and some odd thousand now. It's quite a migration from the East there in Texas, especially to Austin.
From east Texas?
No, from the eastern states. New York, and so on.
Oh, yeah? What's the main -- I mean, what do people work in there? What's the main thing that keeps Austin going?

Well, they have several products -- I think the biggest thing is construction. Highways and buildings, homes, and like that. They do have some of the bigger companies moving there, like Texas -- the company that makes those adding machines, and so on.
Texas Instruments.
Texas Instruments, they have a big firm there. Oh, I can't even think of some of the others. But a lot of them that originated here in the East.
Was it originally, though -- did it have anything to do with ranching, or oil, or -- originally,

Well, it was supposed to have been nearly centrally located. And then it was named after Stephen F. Austin, who was sort of like the father of Texas. And now it has many assets, as far as the land qualities. In those days, shortly after it was created, there was an oil boom in Luling and Lockhart which is less than 30 miles from Austin.
And they had those great ranches. That's the Cotton Belt, so to speak.
Is cotton grown much around there?
Yes, not as much as before. But it seems that the government has kind of limited them on how much they grow now.
Oh, the government limits the amount, does it?

It seems to be that. You find that -- or maybe because of the value of it, or something, but you'll find that they got that maize, and even rice and stuff, and things growing in Texas, where before they were growing all cotton.
What did your father do?
Well, my father he was -- on my birth certificate it says he was a teamster. That is a dignified word for being a man who worked in the stables. He was more or less a stable boy, who --
Well, doesn't that mean he would -- doesn't a teamster sort of have -- hauling wagons and things? Isn't that --

Well, that would be the term now. But I don't know why they put it down there like that, but on my birth certificate it says "teamster." And I know that he was a horse trainer. He'd take the colts and train them to pace, or holler and gee, or whatever, you know. He'd train them for saddling, and train them for working the wagon, working the field, and that sort of thing.
Oh, so he progressed from the stable boy?

Well, he did all of that, too. But this surely is a person, now -- when he died, he was a regular farmhand, did all the plowing, and everything. And still worked as a -- for this one man, and one of the baddest men Texas ever had. His name was General Hamby, it's a big family there.
What was this about the General?
General Hamby, H-a-m-b-y. And that was a huge family.
What was he bad at?
Well, he was one of the men that would ride his horse into the saloon and shot out all the lights and the clock, you know. And anybody else that wanted to

protest it, you know. And he was a shot, you know. My father used to, on Sunday afternoons or whatever day they wanted to go out for a ride, father would drive the gig, you know. Mr. Hamby and his wife would sit in the thing, and my father would drive, you know. And they said he could shoot birds off the telephone wire with his pistol. Said, he was just riding along, he and his wife, and pow. (Laughter.) There goes another bird.
That's some way of entertaining your wife.
(Unintelligible)

He was quite a man. And his brother became some kind of deputy, some kind of law enforcement officer. And just before I left Texas, now, he was getting up there. I guess he was around 60 years old, something like that. But he still, although Texas had started to turn away from that Western atmosphere, to more of a cosmopolitan type atmosphere, he still would come down and feed on his black and white horse, had on a black and white vest, black and white pants, black boots, and two .45 black and white pearl handled revolvers. (Laughing.) And they had to take his guns away from him. By then it had become illegal to wear your guns, you know, in Austin.
Well, he just lived a little too long.
Well, I understand, I was just talking
with some of my relatives the other day, and they told me that -- now, I left there in '32, and they said in the '50s he killed three more men.
And he could get away with it?
Well, you know, they say they had him -- put him in a home, or something, and he wrecked that home. He must have been in his 90's, near 100, you know. He couldn't get that wild West out of his blood.
Well, what did your mother do?

Well, my mother was more or less a housewife, but she also did laundry, like that. And she took us with her. And we used to be so ashamed, you know. She'd take the three boys and my baby sister, when she went to washing in those people's back yards. We had to go, too. And that was an effort to be sure we weren't into any trouble in the -- back home.
Well, were you any help to her, as you grew up?

Well, naturally my sister would -- usually they'd take her out and sit her down somewhere, and give her some toys to play with, or something. But one of my brothers was on that old big, black pot that you boil the clothes in. My mother was on the wash, and my other brother and I were on the two rinses, you know. I was on the pot next to my mother,
so that always gave her a chance where she could pop me, you know, when I didn't -- she'd never even raise -- wet hands with soap, and everything, would be right in my --
(Laughter.)
Well, where did you come in this quartet? Were you the youngest?

Yeah, I was the youngest boy, but older than my baby sister. And let me tell you, I used that, too. I really played that thing, took advantage of the fact that I was the baby boy. I used it on everybody I saw. We had to cut wood, you know --
You were small, were you?

Yeah, I was more or less a midget. I was kind of sickly. And I used that, too, you know. My mother would tell me, go out and bring in an armload of wood, and I'd grab my stomach. "My stomach feels bad," you know. If I didn't get the food I wanted, I had another alibi, you know. But it was wonderful living in Austin. Maybe later on I'll kind of expand on that.
Well, where does music come into it? Did your mother play anything, or --

Well, she wasn't really taught as a musician. Her sisters -- there were eight sisters and three brothers. And I think five of her sisters were good musicians. Good Piano players. But somebody loaned my mother one of those
old foot organs. And some songs I remember today, nobody else has played them -- now as I try to play them, I find out how difficult they were.
One I think is an old English song, "He married another, oh dee." (Phonetic).
Oh, yeah, I remember that.

He used to play that song, somehow. And then she used to play a thing about three little babes that She played that for us. were lost in the woods. And those are pretty hard tunes to play. Played and sang those for us.
That was really a poem that people used to recite, where the sparrows came and covered them over with the strawberry leaves.
Right. She used to play those things. And "Boilin' Cabbage", she could just tear that up. You know how to play "Boilin' Cabbage" don't you.
No, what's that?
(Humming.)
Oh, no, I don't know that.
That was more like a reel in the South, and the people would be doing their you know. They played that dance, see.
Well, do you want to talk about your mother's family at this point?
Yes, I'd better get that in now, because -- listen, I have so much to say, that --
Well, that's good. You might just sort of read from those notes, I think.

Well, first of all, my grandmother owned a restaurant in Texas. Down, right in the heart of downtown Austin. And ironically, my father's half-brother owned a restaurant a couple blocks down the street, in the downtown section. But somehow she managed to put -- she gave her kids, if they wanted to go to school, a good education. And she was highly respected. Everybody called her Mother Glasgow, you know. All the races were crazy about her.

And her oldest son was not a Glasgow. His name was Griffin. I don't know whether she was married before, or whether these were born out of wedlock, I can't say. But two of the kids, the oldest son and the oldest daughter were Griffins. And Buddy Griffin was a prize fighter. He was known as Kid Griffin. He lived in California. And the sister lived in San Antonio. But then the rest of them were all Glasgows, seven girls and two boys.

And she brought them up, evidently, in the church, and they must have done a lot of singing and playing, you know. Because my aunt, only surviving of those sisters, of my aunts and uncles, just recently retired as the organist for Ebenezer, the largest black Baptist church in Austin.
She must have been pretty old?
She's about 92 now. They had quite a
celebration for her when she retired, and everything. But she had the number one choir there. They had three or four choirs, and she had the number one choir for years.

Now, of course, I had my uncle John, married to a lady by the name of Leela Johnson, who was the first cousin of Jack Johnson, the prize fighter. And their children all were taught -- were sent to music school. Now the oldest girl was Nannie Mae. She played mostly classical music. And ironically, her daughter-- she had one daughter and one son, they lived in Chicago, is a featured artist with the Chicago symphony. And she's also the president of some music association. She travels all over the country. Some kind of music society, or something.
What was her name?
The one that's the president?
This musician one.

Nannie Mae. Like nanny goat. Nannie Mae. Now, her brother was John Glasgow, who was a singer. He didn't play any instrument. And they had a brother, Dude -- we never quite found anything -- any talent in him. He was more or less the comedian in that family.

We had -- they had -- let me see, there was four girls and four boys in that family. And Leela played, and Helen is the only one of that family that's living now. Dodgie and the young daughter, that was named Bunch, but we called -- her show business name was Ivy. Well, now, Dodgie --
Now, what did she do, this Ivy?

Ivy, she played piano and sang. And she -- shortly after I left Texas, she had joined a trio, and they sang at the capital for the legislators, and so forth. And they became pretty prominent. And then she moved to California, and she sang with Floyd Ray and his band. She came to Kansas City and visited me when they were passing through.
Now, was she part of that trio that sang with Floyd Ray?
She was one of the main ones. In fact, she was the part of the trio -- she was the one that sang the songs, the individual songs where they had one vocalist. That was her that sang those.
But who were the other two girls in that trio?
I didn't know them too well. I met them, but I mean --
They were just girls?

Yeah. Ivy, Verne and Vonne. And after Floyd Ray had broken up, as I say, I guess around '45 or something, then my cousin, we called Bunch, Ivy, she got a bass fiddle and started playing it. And they formed a little trio. One of them played the drums, or guitar, or something, and one played the piano, and Bunch played the bass. And they
were very successful. They made a couple of movies, you know, played the bits in a couple of movies, like that.
So really there was quite a strong sort of musical side on the Glasgow side?

On the Glasgow side, and also on the Ramey side, too, except that, you know how it is when your father dies, your mother doesn't tell you too much about those over on your father's side. We got the remnants of it later on. But my grandfather, Jack Ramey, was a whiz on violin. And they said -- funny thing, they said that I took some of it after him, although I never saw him. They said when he played, sometimes he'd have his foot as much as a foot off the ground, patting his foot, you know. And you know, I play patting my feet. I can't play unless I pat my feet, you know.
My mother told me, she said, you know, you got that from your grandfather.
Your father didn't play anything?

My father played a little banjo, but he was an athlete, and he sang in the quartet. As did my brother. Now, my brother was with the famous quartet in Texas, the most famous quartet in Texas. And my brother was also a prize fighter, my oldest brother.
How far did he get?
He had won the lightweight championship.
But he had a fractured rib, and it was pressing against his heart, and the doctor told him he'd better stop it. If he got another blow, that could stop his heart instantly.
What did he do after that?

Well, he sang in the quartet, and he took a job as a shoeshine boy. He worked at odd jobs, and things. But that was about his only talent, because I think he left school in the 6th grade. You know, in those days, when Jack Johnson became king, everybody -- so I had two brother-in-laws who were prize fighters, or wanted to be prize fighters.

And one of them I remember very well, because he was the joker of the whole town. Now, these things that Sugar Ray developed, in the forties, evidently he was on his way out to do that. But he's a heavyweight. So they say he would throw one punch, and do all kinds of dancing up and down, and somebody caught him when he was up in the air, knocked him all the way out of the ring. That ended his career. But they called him Pip Sweeney. But he was -- they say he put on quite a show. He'd swing one punch and miss you a mile, but he'd make it look so good, you know.
(Laughter.)
He was a kind of showman.
he could miss you look beautiful
So he could look beautiful, but miss by a yard. And they say even when he got knocked out, he had
down there laid out with a smile on his face. He's still in show business.
(Laughter.)

But now, we was kept away on my mother's side, going back to my cousins. Now, they all sang and played. And I had the other cousins that were like Louise Jones. Her husband -- she and her husband were both great musicians. And her son, Paris Jones, was the one that Kenny Dorham actually learned from. They were like brothers. And when Diz came to Texas, he'd always look for my second cousin, Paris Jones
Well, what did he play?
He played trumpet, and he was one of the greatest in the United States. But he wouldn't leave Texas. He was a professor, he taught.
Did he play jazz, or legitimate stuff
Diz and them are afraid of him.
Playing jazz. Yeah Kenny Dorham will tell you in a minute, if you want to hear something, he'll say, go down and hear your cousin. But he passed away very young, last year.
But let's see if I can think of --
One thing you missed -- you said that your grandmother came from Madagascar.
She remembers coming from Madagascar, yeah, at the age of four or five.
Well, what were they doing, coming from Madagascar?

Well, she said all she remembers was being put on the ship in Madagascar, whether she had been brought over from the mainland of Africa, or whether she was born on Madagascar, all she remembers is being put on that ship and howled like a monster, sailing.
I mean, that's a long trip. It's not like coming from the West Coast -- from the East Coast -- from the West Coast of Africa.
Yeah, coming all the way around that Horn, or whatever they call it.
Cape of Good Hope?

Yeah. So she remembers the Madagascar. And when she got to be 12 years old, the master -- they let her stay with her mother until she was 12, or about 12, she didn't know, because she didn't learn to read until --
How far back would that be in time?
I would have to say that would be somewhere around 1840, or something like that. In the forties, anyway. And maybe before that. Because she had lots of children, and --
Well, when you get to your age, and you have a grandmother that you remember, that can be a long way back.

Yeah, I was fortunate in having -- I can say I was fortunate now. Then I hated it. Being little, my mother always found something for me to do. And one of my chores was to go over there and see about my grandmother, every afternoon after school. So I had to go over there and get all the weeds out of her garden. And after she had retired from the restaurant, she would make big pots of soup. And baby dove -- baby pigeon, what you call that? Squab?
Yeah.

And I'd have to put that under my arm and take it to the city. Sometimes it would be some doctor, some white person we owe, and other // it was out of town, it seemed like she'd search and find out who was sick, and send me to take it, you know. And I had a chance to sit and talk with her a lot.
But still at that age, I guess that was an irritation to you.

Yeah, I had some other things to do. Listen, I wanted to go out and sit there under the tree. By the way, my brother and I when we were young, we had planned on opening a business of our own. Tree setting surgeon business. He was going to set out the tree, and I was going to sit under it.
(Laughter.)
And the reason for that, he said I was the laziest

guy in the world, so he said he was going to go into the gardening business, you know, and part of his business would be setting out trees. And he said he'd let me come around and sit under them. Because that's all I would do.

But you know, when you have chores like that, for your grandmother, or whatever, you -- theoretically you've got nothing to do as a child. I mean, there's all kinds of things you want to do, like play games.

Well, I always managed to get out of there quickly. I'd go as fast as I could, so I could get back and have time. Seemed like the evenings were long. I lived right near the school, and I'd get back home, maybe by 3:00. Five or ten minutes after three, and get out of my clothes and go to my grandmother's, maybe an hour later I'd be back, playing marbles with the rest of the guys. And some of the other games, you know.

But I did have a chance to sit and talk with her. I think -- although in later years, she told somebody in my family that some Indian man, and I understand that my grandfather, John Glasgow, was half-Comanche Indian, that she was rescued from -- they had a parade in San Antonio, Texas, and they were marching along there. Some Indians snatched her out of the parade, and the woman put her up under of her dress and kept her there. She was about 13 or 14 years old. Made her stand right there, and the police couldn't find her. Now,
that kind of seems like it's a little bit out. but one of my sisters told me that she had told her that.

I can't see how they wouldn't -- you know, although it might have been so many of those Indians there. But she was a -- if that is the case, then she was married to John Glasgow, who has enormous relatives in Texas.
We ought to spell Glasgow, that's --

G-l-a-s-s-c-o. And there are oodles of them. In fact, here in New York there's a strange thing. And while I was living here in New York, I called a lady, her name was Glasco, and she lived about four blocks from me. And I asked her, I said, are you Miss Glasco, and she said, yes. And so I said, well, my name is Glasco, and I just wondered if we're any relations. She said, listen, what you trying to pull some hype on me, or something?
(Laughter.)

So I never bothered her again. But she still lives up there in the Bronx. But I would imagine that she's related. Because since I've been home, I've found out there was just a crew of Glascos that live up in the Mahara (PHONETIC) area, which is about 80 miles from Austin, just a little bit southeast of Waco, you know. There's lots of them there.
Well, in Texas there are probably all related anyway.
One way or the other.
Sure. Well, where did you -- when did you begin to get interested in music, yourself?
Well, having all that music around me, when we started -- I guess when I was born. My father died on the farm.
How old was he when he died?

Either 42 or 44. I was three years and nine months old. But I do still remember my father. I do remember that I wore dresses. And when he'd come home, we'd be at the front gate waiting for him. And he'd take us down to the store and buy us some candy, you know, my baby sister and I. Seemed like it'd take us an hour to get down there and back, you know. My baby sister was about a year and a half old, but she was walking, you know.

And when he died, I remember that old, brown, wooden casket, and somebody picked me up and held me there to see him, you know. And I kept saying, 'Why doesn't he wake up and take me to get some candy,' you know, even though he was gone.

But we were surrounded with that music down there. The Glascos, who I was speaking of before, Aunt Eula and Uncle John's children, they and their children would go with us to pick cotton, out at the farm where my father worked year-round, see. And --
(End of Reel 1 as recorded.)

You sign that piece of paper, and they --
(Inaudible).
Now I forget, what I ~ are we -- ?
We were going to talk about how you got started in music, I think.
Well, I -- where we were, I think I can remember, our families went to -- would go pick cotton every year.
That's right. That's where we were.
And when we finished picking, we would sit out in front of that cabin until maybe midnight, singing telling stories, you know, songs, down in Missouri. And we harmonized.
This would be the cabin at the farm?
Yeah.
Where you were going to sleep?
Yeah, where we would -- those two families would stay in that one big thing. All it is the ladies - there is only two rooms, all the ladies in one room, and all the men in the other.

But we'd sit out there and sing. All the spirituals, and all those old good church songs, and some funny songs. Of course, my brothers and them were in the famous quartets And I think I began to get it there. And actually, I composed

my first song, which has never been written, when I was five years old. At that time I had turned out to be not only the sickly one of the group, but I was the preacher of the group. I was -- I had almost been ordained, then. Everybody knew I was going to be a preacher, because I could get out and preach when I was five years old.
I could tell ghost stories and scare all them, and scare myself more.
(Laughter.)
When : You said you were sickly, what was the matter with you?
Well, that part of my alibi started sure enough. // I had this, taking affection. I don't know, it was like a weak stomach. I couldn't eat any kinds of greens.
: You really were not so strong?
Not so strong. And I loved greens, but I couldn't eat any mustard or collards or cabbage. String beans, anything like that. But I finally got so I could.

But anyway, my song was -- I'm going to sing this [said facetiously] to you, because I have such a beautiful voice. It has a different rhyme, a different rhythm and everything to it, but it goes, "I went down the street, and saw some pretty women, don't anybody care about me. Went down the street and I had patches in my pants, don't anybody care about me. I woke up one morning and I had cornbread and beans, don't nobody care about me.
I woke up this morning and I had wet in the bed. My mother beat my back so bad, it sure did hurt."
(Laughter.)
That was --
That led up to a big spanking.
(Laughter.)

So that was my first composition. And they used to ask me to sing that song and then I'd sing it all over. Then I'd get out there, and I could preach. I could roar, and I could get down there and say, "Oh, brother, don't you want to go to heaven?"
Oh, you really did sort of preach?
Yeah, listen, I'd get out there, they'd sing a song and I'd be out there. Sometimes while they were singing, I'd be doing it, you know. I'd commenting.
Well, was this something you picked up from going to the church?

Going to church, sure. And see, we had whole lots of what they called camp meetings in and around us. In fact, they had the St. John's Association every summer, and there was a Holiness church that had a camp meeting, that was about a block from our house. In fact, my brothers used to help park the cars for the white people. You know, they'd come out there in droves, just to watch and listen to those
do the, people sing and shout, and speak the unknown tongue, and all that, you know.
It was like (inaudible). Entertainment.

Yeah. Oh, man, that place, it was out in a great big pasture, and that place would be full of white people. And naturally, the church appreciated that, because they got a good collection everynight, you know. But the people were there, and --
Well, what -- in those days, would the white people and the black people be mixed up, or would they sort of be --
No, there was always that line. But now, you see, they, in things like that, the white people would not come into the tent.
Oh, I see. got you.

They would stand outside the tent. And the black people would stay out of the way so they could see. There were black people there to witness, too, but they would probably get along this side, or on that side, and so the white people could see, you know.
Same way at the dances, you know. They had that although rope. And it seemed that whenever they had bands coming in -- well, I'm getting off on a tangent now, you noticed that.
Yes, but well, we were --
We'll get back to that other.
We'd better get back to that cabin where you're singing, now.

Singing. I began to learn to sing. I used to -- this cousin Helen, and my sister Ethel, used to sing with what was known as The Alto. And I was so crazy about them anyway, and I'd get right in between them, and I'd try to sing their voice. I was throwing everybody off, but I stayed right in the middle of them, and learned to sing their voice. Sing right along. They would tell me, get out of the way, you're throwing us off. But I stayed right there until I learned. Several of us were doing it, but we enjoyed it.

And you know, the funny thing about Texas, it's such a Plains country, that when we stopped singing, we could hear another family maybe three miles away singing. So at times we would all get together and sing, like that.

Then we had -- my brothers and my cousins would all get together. They'd form a ring, a circle, and they would clap their hands, you know. Now each one at a time would get out there in the middle and do a buck dance. They call it getting off the puppy's tail.
Getting off the puppy's tail?
Yeah, getting off the puppy's tail, that's the way, that certain way they'd dance. And they'd sort of glide like -- well, like Baby Lawrence
refined it, you know. But it was that kind of stuff. It was actually flatfooted, you'd hear plop, plop, plop, plop, plop plop, that sort of thing. (Laughter) Yeah, that sort of thing.
But I take it that some of them could do it very well.
Well, you know, my older brothers, they all were very good at it. And they got so they could do -- they had little team things that they would do together, you know, and that sort of thing.
It would be a bit competitive, I take it. Trying to see who could --
Outdo the other, yeah. And then at the end they would all get together, and some particular step that they could all do together, they would do that, you know.
And at the same time they, my brothers and my cousins, they'd sing in quartets. And then this Ira Glasgow, he went on to sing in that Deluxe Melody Boys Band.
Well, now, where did they operate?
They were in Austin, and around, but they did some touring, you know.
Deluxe Melody Boys?
Melody.
Melody.
Deluxe Melody Boys.
Did any famous people come out of

Well, I don't know whether Buddy Tate came there to work with them or not. Herschel -- and I worked with Herschel in Texas, and I didn't do much, because I couldn't play, you know. But I was going through the motions.
Herschel , he was with another band.
What you're talking of here with I mean the Deluxe Melody Boys, this is when? Around '28, or something? How old would you be?
Well, the Deluxe Melody Boys would and went be -- I guess they started about '26 up to until about 1930, or '31.
And this would be around Austin, mostly, would it?
Yeah, they was all local musicians. And then George Corley (PHONETIC) took it over, and that it became George Corley and his Royal Aces.
How do you spell Corley?
C-o-r-l-e-y.

And being in the Boy Scouts -- the one thing I can say, I have to say that in Austin we were very blessed, something that very few others cities here that I think had, we had in Austin.

To keep us out of trouble they had -- the churches had little basketball teams, and little sandlot baseball teams. I think it's possibly something to do with the fact that Austin was the capital city.
It was known as the Friendly City, and the whites would help to buy us uniforms, and --
Yeah, but you know, it seems very often like the capital, when it does have a sort of slightly more responsible attitude, than just a plain, manufacturing
city, or whatever, you know.

Yeah, that might be the thing. But we had -- the parents would -- well, from the time I guess I was 9 years old, especially in the spring and summer months, there was usually a party we had to go to. And one thing I do remember mostly, is that every Friday night, as soon as school was out, until time for school to start, there was a band concert in the park. Brass band?
Brass band, yeah. But it was about 20 pieces. And those people, they were all black, you know, and

they seemed to be so devoted. In fact, Mr. Timmons, who was the bass horn player, was the only teacher I had in Texas on my musical instrument. And he -- I think he was the only bass horn player, and there was about 20 -- might have been two bass horn players, but he's the only one I know. He was a barber in town.
But they had -- they found some activities for us to do. Kept us out of trouble. Helped us to at least see the right direction.
Well, also it was sort of educative, too, wasn't it?
Very much so. Yeah.
Well, did you say you went on to tuba?

And then I found that the baritone horn was too much in between. Because I wanted to either learn to play melody or play the bass -- I mean, you know, play the accompaniment. So then I got a tuba. I got an E flat (PHONETIC).

Yeah.

No, because this is -- the trumpet is usually right on the tip of the center of your lip. And that means the muscles have to develop on either side to keep the air from going out, and that was my trouble. When I got to blow a trumpet, air was coming out on both corners of my lips.

Yeah, exciting as it can be. And in those days -- for a guy were playing a lead instrument, and he could play "The Flight of the Bumblebee", he was the greatest. No, it was all balanced.
Then, all of a sudden, signs of progress, something--they started making the bass the dominant figure in the rhythm section. You hardly hear the piano or the drums.
When actually did that happen?

I'd say that started around 1947-48. That started when they started getting noisy, with all those amplifications. You know, when we first started recording, at the most, there would be two mikes in a studio.

Look, I mean, when the sort of "bop" idea of the drums being up on the cymbals, and the-- you know, the bass drum is sort of no longer--just a matter of punctuating, the bass has gotta carry the thing a little more, hasn't it?

Yeah, and that really isn't the thing. You know, if you think of the assignments each of those instruments is supposed to have, the drummer's hired to carry the tempo. That's his only thing; he can decorate, but his job is to carry the tempo.
Yeah.

I've had that argument--not argument, but discussion with several drummers who say, "Well, man, you know that bass player rushes the tempo, or that bass player pulls the tempo back." Well, that isn't the thing. You hold it, you know.
The drummer should hold it?
Yeah, the drummer, that's what he's hired for, to carry that tempo.
Well, then how do you--what do you--since the bass is sort of the foundation?

Yeah? Well, you see, back in the --when bop came in, this is why Curly Russell and I were the most hired guys on fifty-second street, 'cause this is when the drummers began to put their foot in their pockets.
Right.

And I don't care how fast the tempo was, or how difficult it was or how ragged it got, they had to have a strong bass player to carry that beat while the drummer, instead of carryin' the tempo, he was decoratin' and actually, stealin' the solo from the horns in places. But it became such an exciting thing that they accepted it, you know. But now this was created by the Basie rhythm section, by the man that I adore most, 'cause he actually made that Basie a rhythm section. That's what he used to tell 'em.

Yeah.

Yeah.

Yeah.

Right.

I mean, that would be something that they'd hear.

Wellman Braud was strong.

No.

That's it.

60 feet. Oh, oh, oh.

Well, at this time, we're talking of what--'33?

Yes.

Yeah.

Yes.
That sort of thing.

Yeah. He had kinda loosened up. Now Ben Webster had not developed that style at all. In fact, I don't even think that he had developed it when he was with Teddy Wilson. I think Duke Ellington brought that out of Ben.
Well, look, I mean, once you do it==
He and Johnny Hodges and those guys --

--as compared with the others.
Yeah. Well, they were busy running, but I would say that at that time, everybody kinda' thought that Dick Wilson was next for President in Kansas City.

Yeah. One thing I do remember might've been the thing that they held against him. He liked to play lots a' high, screaming notes--not as high as Jackie but --

--he liked to play lots of the higher parts of the saxophone, you know.
Oh.
But he--
Well, I mean was Lester playing tenor then with that sort of light tone?
Yeah, he was playing that tenor with the alto style.
Well, did you like that?
Well, I did. But, you know, everybody was a Coleman Hawkins fan.
Right. That's what I mean.
And it was in '33 when we went over
there and saw that music ?, you know, when they needed somebody to take Hawk's place in Fletcher Henderson's band.
Right.

Right.
--ability to execute. Tell us a story, and don't let it be a lie. Let it mean something. If it's only one note, like Louis Armstrong, like Duke would do, you know, with that 'lu'?

--and Fletcher fired him right away.

I worked in a shoeshine parlor in the daytime and worked at nights when I had a gig, you know, with the groups. So at noon all of us would make it to that Chinese restaurant where they had that radio on. We'd hear that band coming from the Gunter Hotel. And then we could get, from time to time, Alphonso Trent (phonetic) coming from that hotel in Dallas--I just called the name of it?
Adolphus.
Adolphus Hotel.
Yeah.
And--
Now was that, in that time, a good band?
Alphonso Trent? Yeah! Listen, you know, sometime it could be the music ability, and it could be the socializin' ability.
Yeah.
Now, Basie's band really built

theirs up on socializing. I mean that big following in and around Kansas City and them places. Now, because that whole band didn't believe in going out with a sidety black people. They'd head straight for pimps and prostitutes' table, they'd hang out with them. And those people were great advertisement for Basie. Like, they didn't dig--I won't say dig--but they said Andy Kirk was too uppity, you know.
Yeah. Prim and proper.

Yeah. And Basie was down there layin' in the gutter with them. You'd see Basie with patches in his pants and everything (laughter), right down there with them, gettin' drunk, and all of Basie's band was like that.
Yeah.
Anyway, you can still see that in Joe Jones, like he goes wherever there's a gang hanging out, you know.
Yeah.
And, uh--I'm gettin' away again. Listen, I'm goin' more on tangents.

Well, let me think. Yes, I know we've talked about Countess Johnson, and you said she sounded rather more like an Earl Hines. And I was saying I supposed that Earl Hines was a big influence on Kansas City because of radio.
Well, he was all over --I'd say
the United States. You see, I don't know whether you ever heard this or not, but some magazine or somewhere they showed how Earl Hines could stretch those tenths.
Yeah.
And so guys--it was like a conventional saying, you know. The reason Earl Hines I know how he could stretch those tenths like that, he had his fingers split.
The webs cut:
The webs cut. Did you hear that, too?
They just put that to (inaudible) his webs cut. holding his hands up to show he didn't have them split.
He didn't have his webs. So it was all over, and everybody was tryin' to stretch those tenths like Earl Hines (laughter), y'know.
Yes.
And so I'd say he was a bigger influence out there than anybody until after, say maybe, Jelly Roll Morton or maybe--what was it, General Moos (phonetic) somebody?
Well--
Who played with New Orleans style ?
Yes.
I mean some of those first
baretelhouse piano players.
Yeah.
Yeah. Well, the next one was Earl Hines.
Yeah.
Definitely. And, in fact, you spoke of my lady there, and soon as we got there, she asked a bellhopper, "Is Mr. Hines still here?"
Well, I had come in to reserve your room.
Yeah, I told that they had--
Yeah, 'cause I told him, you know--I was speaking to him, and I said you're coming in Wednesday, so he said he'd reserve it.
Uh-huh.
Is it okay, apart from the door?
What? Yeah, everything's fine now, except that door.
Oh.
And I had a screechy bed all last night.
He always has to check out his T.V. when he comes in here, and make sure he has good color T.V.
Yeah.
Yeah.
If it isn't, he'll move, you know.
Uh-huh. Yeah, everything's all right up there. And so everybody all over the country was patterning after Earl Hines.
Yeah, well, you can hear it in Basie--the early records of Basie, Mary Lou, and--
Yeah.
Well, how long did this gig with Countess Johnson last?
Well, now we stayed together until she took Mary Lou's place with what's-er-name.
Yeah.
With Andy Kirk. She came to New York and I mean, she didn't live long after that.
Oh. That's a shame.
Yeah, I don't know whether it was '37 or '38.* But anyway, they brought her back home, and very shortly after that, she died. She made one record with Billie Holiday.
Yeah?
Uh.
I didn't know that. I don't think so, Gene.
I think you'll find that she made
*According to Chilton's WHO'S WHO OF JAZZ, Countess Johnson died in Kansas City in the summer, 1939.
it--I'm pretty sure that she made it with Billie Holiday.
Well, what was her name, apart from Countess?
Margaret Johnson.
Margaret Johnson.
Well, I'll look it up.* I don't--
I'm pretty sure because--Prez is gone, but I'm pretty sure--he was crazy about her. And I believe he got her on that.
If he did, it's an interesting point. I mean, you know, it's surprising how many times she's mentioned in books and things like that.
Uh-huh.
But I mean, you know, there's just a name; it doesn't mean anything.
Yeah, well, she was very, very powerful. And then, going on from that, she's got a brother that plays piano now, that was a bass player with Lionel Hampton.
Yeah?
Uh-huh.
What's his name?
Roy Johnson.
Oh, that's her brother.
Uh-huh.
Where does he play and work now?
*Both the Rust and Bruyninckx discographies indicate Holiday recorded in September, 1938 with a Margaret "Queenie" Johnson in New York.
He's in Kansas City playing piano.
Yeah?
And when we left there, he was playing piano, like she was. But after I left there, next time I saw him, he was playing bass with Lionel Hampton.
(chuckle)
Is he--was he good?
I thought so. He was in there when Hamp (phonetic) had some of his better bands, after the original band, you know.
What was the other Johnson, though, that played piano--Everett Johnson, who--?
Everett Johnson. Now--
Who was he?

Everett Johnson was one of those cats that could get out there and stretch out on Pete Johnson, and they'd battle all night. Yeah. He could really play barrelhouse and play some eight-to-the-bar blues and all that, you know.
Well, the time we're talking of, Pete Johnson was well known by then, was he?
Yeah, he was. But I think Everett was a little bit mo' popular.
Oh, before Pete?
Yeah.
Oh.
You know, a whole lot has to do with who chooses who.
Yeah.
You know. For an example, when Andy Kirk was winnin' all the battles, when Basie came in and won such acclaim. But he had the right publicity and everything behind him, Basie, you know.
Yeah.
But Andy Kirk, he didn't have the right people that really cared enough to give him a build-up, you know.
Well--
Basie ended up with Benny Goodman and John Hammond behind him--
Well, that's the point, isn't it?
Yeah, and that put them right on top. But Andy Kirk was the most popular band in Kansas City as far as the--
I mean, the thing is, that at the same time, it doesn't seem to me, it was a rather pretty band when Mary was playing with it, but it didn't really have the drive of Basie's, did it?
Well, I put it a different way. I say that there are some bands, and I could name some other Kansas City Bands, who have too much orchestration.
Yeah.
There are two hornists, you know.

Basie's band was generally made up of a first and last chorus. And then Buster Smith, Herschel or Jack Washington (phonetic) or one of those four guys in the reed section set those riffs (phonetic), you know.
Yeah.
And if you listen to those original Basie records, and how they sound so exciting? And sometime it wan't really a solo that made that thing so exciting, it was that riff that was backin' him up.
That's right.
And, now that also left them free-- the horns wasn't fightin' to make that note on time and everything.
Don't you think that was very often the case in those days?
Like, in those real experienced bands, with Duke and Luneford and Andy Kirk, sometime.
Yeah.

But now, I'll show you one band that you found that came from New York, and they really didn't make it 'cause they didn't do enough playing ad-lib. And that was Harlan Leonard. His band was too much arrangement.
Yeah.
And this is how we outblew them
all the time, 'cause they were playing arrangements, and Mac Shann (phonetic) would give us the first chorus and turn us a'loose, you know.
Well, when did you get with Mac Shann, then?
I was about, well, I think it was either the 18th or the 28th of April, 1938.
Oh, it's as late as that? So we've got four years to go, then?
Yeah.
Now what do you do after this thing with Countess Johnson?

Well, now, we--after Countess left, there was a guy who--I can't think of his name-- I'm still workin' at Western University--who came down from Flint, Michigan. Now he had a band in Kansas City before that. Can you think of any of the bands that came from Kansas City then? This guy, after he broke up, he moved to (unintelligible), got him a state job in Flint, Michigan.
Uh, yeah, I know of some people--
I can't put a finger on it right now.
It's not —, uh, yeah, Eddie Barefield (phonetic) had sump'n to do with that band, didn't he?
Uh-huh. I think so, yeah.
Yes, I think so. I know he was up that way.
Well, that guy came down to Kansas City. I went into a walkathon. Now, see, we were playing all kinds a'gigs.
Yeah.
And I took that job with walkathon. He brought some Michigan musicians with him and he hired me on bass, you know. And that was bangin' twenty-five a week, you know, which--
Clarence Chance (phonetic) Johnson, Eli Rice, Grant Moore, Zach White, he went out to the West Coast?
No. This guy's just died a few years ago. You got anything of Kansas City bands?
No, I merely had this book of people, you know.
Oh, he had a pretty nice band there at one time. well, this band was like--you heard of--
Who else was in it?
I didn't know too much of the individuals. Julius Banks and Paul Banks, you heard of them? Their--
Yeah.
--band in Kansas City? Well, his band
was like on that level--
Oh.
--wan't up to par with the swingers, you know.
Oh.

But I went to work with him, and I worked with him for a short while, then I went with Bus Moten. See, now, when Benny Moten died, you know, well, there was a big rift there. You probably have that in the records somewhere, don't you?
I think we'd better just let me change this because--
All right.
We're gonna talk about Moten and stuff.
Yeah, well, did we finish enough with Earl Hines and (unintelligible) and them?
Yeah, you said that.
I mean, this is almost a do-it-yourself thing. There are people who listen to Walter Brown, and you know, they almost feel they can sing that well themselves.
Yeah. Well, he had even a bad talking voice. He was completely nasal, you know.
Yeah, very nasal.
And he didn't use good diction. In fact, you could -- some people could misunderstand what he said when he said, 'Baby, Here I Stand Before You,' you know. 'With my heart in my hand.'

Even when you've said that, though, there was something personal about it. You know? I can understand why they liked him. But when Jay sings the same things in more or less the same way, he sings them better.
Oh, yeah. Well, he's got a musical --
of course he can,
Yeah, that's what it is. But personally,
Jay can sing in that same nasal way.

Yeah, he can sing in a nasal way, but you can hear him singing the tunes and the melodies, you know. Like what we admire about Frank Sinatra, Frank Sinatra can sing a tune -- and sing it as the notes are written.

It was a good thing she did, really, because I think she would have had trouble with Goodman anyway.
So we're talking about what happens after Countess Johnson's (PHONETIC)?
Oh, yeah. I almost had this man's name.
Well, it will come.
we went to that walk-a-thon. You know what a walk-a-thon is? See, those people who can outlast each other, and they walk so many hours a day.
Where did they walk?
This was at a place called Playmore Ballroom. Now, Playmore Ballroom was a place where no Negroes were allowed before that. They brought in all the good bands, you know, I mean the white bands.
White bands?

Yeah. And we played there. But it happened that this company had hired the -- had rented the hall and caused Playmore to cancell out his other engagements when they found the guy was bringing a black band in. It was too late to do anything about it, you know. So anyway, all we did was to come in the back door and go up there on that thing and play, you know.
How big a band was this, then?
I think this was four or five pieces.
Oh, that small?
And all we did was just go up there and play some kind of music while the other people would go around

that thing. Sometimes on skates and sometimes walking, you know, just going around this little arena. And sometimes they'd make them dance with each other, and everything. Or they'd be walking asleep, you know. It was an endurance thing, you know.
Well, how long would they walk?
Well, the contest would end when the last -- the next-to-last people fell out. And I don't remember just how long that was. We did that again with Jay McShann, too.
Well, they would walk, I take it, for a couple days, wouldn't they?
Oh, couple of days! Sometimes it would last for three or four weeks!
Well, you just went and played sometimes?

Yeah, we went in the afternoon and night and played, and the rest of the time they'd get some record players going, you know. Then they only had to do this for so many hours, you know. So maybe they'd get up at 2:00 o'clock in the morning and start walking, you know.
Oh, I see, they didn't walk all the time.

Not all day and night, no. And they probably had people thinking they were walking all day and night, because a certain time they let the audience come in to see them, they made them start walking a little bit before
we got there, you know.
Well, this was during the period when everybody was sitting on poles, and things?

That's right. Doing that at the same time. And see, now, this turned out more or less to be the offshoot of those carnivals and things that the bands used to do before. See, it used to be when that medicine man came around, going through town, whatever, the weird, the two-headed man, and the billy goat that had a dog's head on it or something, and they'd build a tent somewhere and they'd have a band.
Well, that was when the band used to have to do that promenade, you know. And we had to do that. So now we're jumping way back, but like I say, this was an offshoot of those --
Yes, I see. Well, of course it did have a slightly different purpose, didn't it? I mean, it was accompaniment to the people walking. And also, the people who were there watching, it was something --

To entertain them, too, yeah. And it brought everything, really, indoors. Very seldom, really, that you had a walk-a-thon that was out in the open. It was usually some, a indoors, in a firm establishment. Where they wouldn't have any trouble with people sneaking in, they had to come in through the main entrance, or somewhere.
You mentioned that this Playmore was white only. What was the Cherry Blossom?
The Cherry Blossom was -- it was the old Eblon Theatre.
Avalon?

E-b-l-o-n. Eblon. And you remember in the previous years, Basie and this guy, O'Taylor, used to play there. They played this accompanying music while the silent movie, or something, was showing. And Basie played the organ and this guy played the violin.
Well, what happened to the -- I mean, when it became the Cherry Blossom? Was it a dance hall then, or --

It had become one of those huge night-clubs. And this was on Vine Street, between 18th and 19th, directly across the street from the Booker T. Washington Hotel, which by that time had become the most popular one for musicians, you see. And next door to it -- across the street from it was Lucille's when she had her first club. Before she moved around on 18th Street. And next door to it on the right was a club known as the Kentucky Tavern. And that's where jam sessions would usually start around 2:00 o'clock in the afternoon, spook breakfasts, we called them in Kansas City, you know.
Spook breakfasts?
Yeah. And that was anybody who'd stay up all night. We called them spooks, you know.
Well, I thought that was an insulting term for blacks.

And sometimes it was, you know, but not understood as that in Kansas City. In what's his name -- the term that was used in Kansas City was more or less the ghost, you know, the spook. Anybody who stayed up that late was a ghost.
Yeah, I got you.

Well, for example, if I can give you a little turn of my life, the name Jay McShann has, Hootie, you know, now they used to say that he'd drink some whisky and then he would hoot like an owl, you know. He'd stay up so late that he was up with the Hoot owls.
Oh, it has nothing to do with hootch then?
No. It was like he was up with the owls all night.
Oh, I thought that was --
Yeah, like old Hootie, you know. That owl, he's out there again tonight.
But he did have a reputation for drinking, too, didn't he?
Yeah.
Well, we'll come to him. Let's go on
from the walk-a-thon. Where did you go from there?
The walk-a-thon, after I left that I went with the -- Benny, Bus Moten Group. (unintelligible)
That's right. That's where we're getting to.
And I worked with them for a small time. Then I just gigged around when gigs came.
What sort of group did Bus Moten have then? Benny Moten had died, hadn't he?

Yeah, Benny Moten died, and see, these guys were trying to get that Reno club after Basie left, see. By this time Basie had gone to New York, you know. In fact, he'd been gone for some time. But anyway, it was in '36 or '37.
'36? '36 Basie went.
Or early '37. I think it was '37, because I kind of remember, I only had one kid, my daughter.
Now, when you were there -- you were in Kansas City before Benny Moten died?

Yeah, I was there. In fact, I was over there in front of the union the day they took their picture in '34. You see the picture of them where they were in front of the union? It happened that we were playing a club, what was that man's name that was head of the union? He came down and threatened us. We were at the 12th Street Taproom playing, and he came down and threatened us, we'd better join the union

or he was going to come up there and tear up all our instruments. So we had to come over there and talk to him. Because this job we had was just a thing, a one-night shot. We were playing three nights there, and we didn't know when we were going to get another job, you know.
Well, where did Benny Moten work mostly?

I think that they had those parks, there was Winwood Beach out there and there was Fairland Park. And it seems to me that Winwood Beach was in north Kansas City and Fairland Park was in the southern part of Kansas City. Same kind of things. And then he was on the road.
But then in those days, around Kansas City and those places, those guys booked themselves, you know. Like McShann's band did in later years.
Well, you couldn't work all the year in Kansas City?

No, none of those bands stayed in Kansas City that long. I don't know if they booked it themselves or not -- if I can retract a little bit, back there -- retrace a little bit, in Texas we'd see George E. Lee come in with those big, beautiful cars, and Benny Moten would come in. Farl Hines only came once, but just like every three months you'd see those bands coming in there. King Oliver would be down, Louis Armstrong and his band would be down. Cab Calloway would come down.
Well, Duke was down there in '33 at the World's Fair or something. Oh, you'd be up in -- (Unintelligible)
Yeah, I was in Kansas City then.
(Inaudible). That's the first time he went.
But --
Well, Earl would have gone down there, too, wouldn't he?

Yeah, we saw Earl. Earl was in demand everywhere. Everybody was trying to get him at the same time. They'd even take him on a Monday morning if they could have gotten him. But they -- all those bands out of Kansas City had -- I don't know whether they had somebody booking them, or what, but they had a regular tour.
A circuit?

Yeah. And everytime they came down, they stole another one out of Texas, musicians, or Oklahoma musicians, you know. That's how they got Lips, and guys from Oklahoma. In fact, I can say this, Earl Hines was most famous for stealing members out of the band. I think McShann put it mildly when he said that Earl Hines came to him and offered him some money, you know.
Well, I think so, too, because somebody told Hines -- I think in the book I did on Ellington, Willie Cook said that Jay McShann was real upset with what Earl did to him in Boston.
Yeah.
But I think Willie also said that at that time McShann was not doing very well.

Well, McShann wasn't too happy because most of the time I had the band. In other words, McShann was being harrassed by the Army. I shouldn't say being har-rassed, but everytime you looked, they were calling him down for induction.
Well, just turning back now, what have we got to fill in finish before McShann? Now Did you work for a time with Bus Moten? Bus was playing piano, was he?
Yeah, and sometimes he would play accordion, you know. Sometimes he would take jobs where there wasn't a piano, then he'd take an accordion and play it.
Well, how did you like the accordion?

Well, to tell you the truth, I wasn't too fond of either one of them, because I don't think Buster was ever -- I think Buster had formed himself on something -- you know, there's two kinds of piano players, one is a soloist, single piano player, and one plays with the band. And it seemed to me like Buster would start out a tune, and then just go for himself. And if he decided he wanted to play this chord, although this chord here belongs with it, he'd go off with it, you know. That sort of thing.
Now, you did have a little better chance with that
accordion, because he was playing like on the treble side, and you were on the bass. But that piano, when he was playing both hands, it was kind of rough, you know.
Well, was Benny Moten considered a better piano player than Bus?
I would think, yes. Although I never heard Benny do anything -- in solo. When he got Basie, you know, all he did was sit over there on that lefthand side.
Well, from what you hear of the early records, it's not very impressive, you know. It doesn't sound Sounds as though he was a soloist, really.

Yeah, I didn't notice too much his being an outstanding musician, you know. But he was a good organizer, a good manager. He kept his bands together better than anybody else. Now, there is another band that was being robbed, but he was being robbed by the eastern bands, you know. Even Blanche Calloway was still hitting in there. Cab, and all of them.
Well, where did Blanche come from? Oh, she was Cab's sister, wasn't she?
I understand they were both from some part of Missouri.* Cab got her when he first had his band, the Missourians, or something. But I don't know --
That's right. Well, that was a band called The Missourians that he took. That's what Cab did, He took this band over. They were known as the Missourians,
*Blanche Calloway was born in Baltimore in 1904; Cab in Rochester, N.Y. in 1907.
and he had them for -- then he gradually made changes.
But in this band with Bus, how many pieces was that?

That was about eight pieces. And he'd make some arrangements. But see, that was that scuffle now, when everybody was trying to get that Reno Club. Now, Dee Stewart also had a band. He was also -- he had been a first in Benny Moten's band trumpet player. So he was trying to get that Reno Club. I think McShann played with (Dee Stuart.)
Yes, he did. He played at a place called the Continental with him.
Yeah. Now, the Continental -- I can't think of the name of that before it was the Continental.
That was downtown, he said.

Yeah, that was nextdoor to the Muelbach Hotel. We played there. In fact, I was there when Charlie Barnet tried to hire me in '38. But the Continental had another name before that. But they were doing very poorly, and then they started bringing bands in, and they gave it the name Continental. But the same guy, Eddie Spitz and them, Randazzas owned it, you know. Eddie and Jack Landaser.
You haven't up to this point -- where do you meet Walter Page?
Oh, I met Walter Page in 1932 at the battle of the bands. At first he was there with his own Blue Devils, and a week or two later he was there with -- I
saw him with Benny Moten (PHONETIC).
Well, did you learn much from him? I mean, did you spend much time with him, or --

Well, I didn't learn any -- what's the name, technical things from him, as far as playing the bass. But I learned from him how to construct -- how to support a soloist, you know. How to work with a rhythm section. And that was the first thing that became so disgusting with me when our rhythm section had to break up, and I had to come here to New York and work with various drummers and piano players every night, you know. And see that these guys didn't have the restraint.

What he showed me most of all was restraint, you know. I had to stand back there in that door -- this door was like leading to the alleyway, where he had to stand. But most of the time they had it closed. I'd stand right back there, right next to him, and he'd tell me, he'd say, now, there's a whole lots of things I could do here, but what you must do is play a straight line, because that man out there's waiting for this food from you, you know. And so he said, you could run all the changes, you could run changes on every chord that's going on. He said, you've got time to do it. But he said, if you do, you're interfering with that guy. So run a straight line.
Then he told me that generally speaking, if you've got a slow tune and the melody goes up, usually you should
ordinarily go down. The bass should run his line down. If the melody is coming down, then the bass should go up as a whats its name, which helps to put the body in it.

And he taught me such things as building the second chorus. And how to avoid, when you see you're getting in a clash with another man in the section, you know, for an example, sometime you might find a drummer that's gotten on the wrong beat, you know. And he showed me like go into a Latin beat, or some kind of -- accents and the thing where you won't interfere with the piano, you won't interfere with whats the name, and you rest of them, but wait and let him catch up, find each other, rather than to stay out there and show him up.
So things like that he showed me.
Well, that was fairly -- I mean, he was much more experienced than you at that stage, wasn't he?

Yeah. And I value that better than any -- I didn't have too much real music training, teaching, anyway. Because I bought a chart, it was a Frank Skinner book, and in the middle of that book was a chart to paste on a bass fiddle. When I first got that bass fiddle I got that chart and I pasted it on the bass fiddle. And it showed the names of each note, and where your fingers should be, and all. And I'd just go home and practice on that.
But I still couldn't it finger it like they -- because of my fingers being double-jointed, you know. But I
found out where the positions were, and I could get on to it.
Did you regard that as a handicap?
Yeah, especially for speed and for endurance, you know.
I was going to say, in a sense it must make it a bit harder work.

It is pretty hard, you know. It's really disgusting, too, because sometimes when you try to play like this, and you when hold your bow, you should really play on the cp ball of your fingers. And you're bowing on something and you find your fingers doing that, give in that stops the note right away, you know. Now, if you've got your strings down low, it won't be as noticeable, but when you're bowing and your finger all of a sudden does that, you get that beep.
How far back do they bend when you press them?
Oh, they go all the way.
Yes, you've got much more give. It's in this joint, isn't it.
It's in both, in this and that.
Yes, but I mean you see it more there.
Yeah, that's the weakest one there, you see. And see, I can put a dime down and pick it up with either one of these joints here. I'm super human. (said facetiously)
But that's where you can sort of see the
effect of the double jointing, on that one, you know. Because that's --

And it used to be that my thumb would do that, too. And when I was younger, my thumb -- I could just do like this and touch my wrist, you know. So I should have joined the carnival instead of the band.
(Laughter.)
They could turn a spotlight on your hands and make a shadow on the wall.
Yeah, they can look real huge, and everything.
Well, this thing with Bus didn't last very long, did it?

No, but this is where I met McShann. We used to go down; we'd meet at that taproom down there on 12th and Paseo Versailles (PHONETIC). And I got jobs around with different ones. I think I made one with Oliver Todd. I know that Thanksgiving -- it was either that Thanksgiving or that Christmas of '37, we had had a job at a place called Smith's Tavern out on 33rd. Smith's Tavern was a huge building. It was evidently an old garage, or something. It was a nice neighborhood at that time.
And we took that job, evidently there was some tough guy that owned that club. And we had a drummer by the name of Bobby Stafford. This being a holiday, and he had a chance

to make a few dollars more on some other job. And he let the bosses know a week ahead that he was going, and the boss told him, don't go. And he went on anyway, and a few weeks, a few days later, we heard that he was in the hospital. They had caught him somewhere on a stroll and beaten him up for doing it. He was, naturally, expecting to do that and then come back with us, but he never showed up again with us. He's still around Kansas City and now we laugh about it all the time.
Who's group was this you went in?
This was with Oliver Todd.
Oh, yeah, Oliver Todd. What did he play, or was he just the leader?
He was a trumpet player.
