We had quite a few blues singers around Kansas City by that time, but they all to us seemed like they were poor imitations of Jimmy Rushing and George Turner.
Yeah, yeah.
So we didn't pay any attention to them, in fact, all the time previously McShann had ballad singers.
Ballad.
Yeah, he had sometimes the men and sometimes the girls --
Oh, yeah.
-- singers. But he didn't hardly fool any of them blues singers.
Well, it was kind of an -- almost an accident that you got sort of pushed into this blues thing so much.
Yeah, we --
Well, I take it that after this record of Confessin' the Blues was such a big hit, you had to.

Yeah, that was something that we had just rigged together a few days before we left. In fact, I think Brown joined us in about January and we were down in Wichita and working, and had a few gigs. And went along, the horns, the reeds and the brass, would work out a little thing to do on the tour. Brown knew nothing about music. He just left it up to us.
Right.
And the thing began to go over good every place we played. We got down to (unintelligible) everyone was crazy about him.
When you played it I take it that you didn't just play it with the trio. The whole band played it.
The whole band played it. And now this was -- there was never one note written on it. In fact, Bird were and I supposed to have written 'Jumpin' the Blues.' Not one
note was written. Down in Wichita -- I mean, down in New Orleans, and we had to get ready for that 1942 recording date?
Yeah.

And we sat down there and started humming riffs that would fit. (unintelligible). And so I got the first eight bars of that and Bird did the last four. And that was the theme of Jumpin' the Blues. Brown came in and sang, and then as we played and rehearsed it, we made up different riffs that would fit with it, and that became the theme after that. Before that, McShann had an old blues theme that is on that record that you heard in Wichita.
Oh.
Remember that thing, Bird was playing that mournful background behind something?
Yes.
Well, that was the theme song. The whole band played that. (Singing.) Now, that might have been the thing that typed us as a blues band.
Yeah.

Because we had to start to using that. But I'll tell you how we got that. We used to -- riding home at night, we used to reminisce about old tunes. There was an old song that somebody sang, that said, (sings) 'well, when my mama's dead and my papa's across the sea,' -- and we used to just enlarge on

that, so this is how this mournful thing got to us. And then as you noticed, sometimes in the solo works the guys would go back to their thing. You listen to the riffs that was played behind it, built off of that.
Well, listen, before Bird went down to the Ozarks with George E. Lee, now, according to Jay, when he comes back, he's really changed a lot.

Yeah, definitely. Well, now, you see, actually, I have to say that I don't think Jay knew him before that because Jay hadn't come to Kansas City. Jay was there when he came back, and Parker met him maybe because he left -- that was in '36 and Jay came in '36. But, say, like, the times when we knew him -- I knew him from early '34, when he was a nothing saxophone player, and we used to go to jam sessions. I used to get him out of there and make him go home and so forth.
Maybe -- of course, that's what Jay meant. He may have meant that he --
He probably had heard the rumor about how bad --
How bad he was.

Yeah, he was a terrible saxophone player. But back in those days, I could always get him to jam with me. And even when we got with Mashann, when I saw he was getting ready to go get himself some drugs or something, I'd tell him, Man, can't you give me 15 minutes, just kind of get
our fingers together?" He'd get down there and I started playing and forget all about those things.

But, now, that thing (unintelligible) is definitely true. When he came back from George F. Lee, and by that time that Jones Smith record had come out, Basie, so that might have been in early '37 because Basie left in '36.
'37, (inaudible), I think.
Yeah, well, --
Well, maybe late '36, yeah.

Yeah. Well, that Jones-Smith record come out and Prez had made that 'Lady Be Good.' And Bird came back and he startled everybody. He hit 'Lady Be Good,' and all the other saxophone players played, and the cats said, yeah, here come this guy, he's a drag. He gets up and plays Lester Young's solo note for note.
Oh, yeah?
Played it note for note, sounded just '... dig that man.' like Prez. And from then on, Bird was gone.
He played it on alto, then.
Played it on alto.
Yeah.
Yeah, note for note. Couldn't believe that. Six months before that, he was, like, a crying saxophone player. Although he had improved from when I heard him in '34.
But you think Lester was a strong influence.

Oh, definitely. You know, if I might say, the influences as they flow -- Louis Armstrong was the influence on Lester Young. Lester Young was an influence on lots of saxophone players and Billie Holiday. You can see that same meaningful sound in what they did. And although one famous writer says that Bird told him he was not influenced by Lester Young, if you listen to him, you can tell that he was completely influenced by him.
And of course Buster Smith was the one that actually made that Basie band, as quiet as its kept.
Well, now, what was Buster's influence on Bird?
You know, now, you remember, when we had jam sessions, we called them spook breakfasts in Kansas City.
Yeah.
What they would do, for example, if a trumpet player is playing, it might be ten saxophone players there and Buster would set a riff. You understand what a riff is?
Oh, yeah.
He'd set a riff. Now, like, you hear the riff being played here, if one horn sets a riff, the other guy plays in unison with him.
Yeah.
But there in Kansas City, it was --
Buster would set that riff, the other horns had to find a harmonic note to play with.
Yeah.

See, so it would sound like a real chorus that was written. You get that in Basie's recordings, you know, when that band was jumping so good. Well, Buster was noted for that. And when he wanted to get you out of there, you got eliminated, you just got to go sit down, you can't play no more for awhile. If you had a bad note in that riff, even though you may have played your solo well, but if you didn't get that thing right with what's its name the first time, you had to get down.

And this was the thing that was most inspiring to Bird, was the fact that he learned so many different kinds of riffs, tricky riffs and things, like, for example, -- I forget the voice, but, say, let's say, Buster would make a riff (bup bup biddly biddly) saying (singing). And the other guys have got to harmonize with that and get that, and if they didn't get the harmonic notes to every one of those things he made, they just eliminated him.
And Buster would do that in a jam session, especially when it got to be too many horns there. He'd set some heavy riffs and the guys would just get their horn and go away and sit down at the table.
That was making them think all the time, too.

Yeah, yeah. And it also showed that a young guy that came in there, he didn't only have to learn how to play a solo, he had to learn how to team. And also, the sections there, they have to breathe at the same time and all that. So this made them have to get together on more than just the solo.
So --
Well, before you go to Buster Smith and Basie, what about Buster Smith as a soloist? Was he a big improvising man himself?
He was a great improviser. He didn't have the strong sound of Hodges or Bird or Benny Carter, like that. He had a soft alto sound, but he was very good as a lead instrument.
Was it more like Hilton Jefferson, or --
No.
Hilton Jefferson's sound was not exactly soft, but it was -- well, yes, it was soft.
Yeah, well, I can think of Buster's sound more as -- remember Charlie Holmes, that used to play with Louis Russell?
Well, he was a Johnny Hodges imitator, really, but it was softer.
It was softer than Johnny Hodges.
Well, really, what Charlie did, he
played like Johnny did in the early days.
Yeah.
That's what it was.
Yeah.
Johnny later got that -- yes.

So Buster was like that. But, now, when they had the spook breakfasts, and Benny Goodman and those guys would come in, what's his name, he'd get his clarinet out and he'd clean everybody out, including Benny.
Oh, yeah?
Oh, yes. He'd clean everybody out that played the clarinet.
People have talked about him on it, I think (inaudible). They've always talked about him on -- sax
On his alto and thing, but he was -- oh, oh, that clarinet.
Well, why did he sort of fade out of the picture? Why was it that Buster didn't become --

Sometimes it might be the powers that be that wanted it, so-and-so, but I think, just like with Lips, they weren't satisfied with what the money was going to be worth, how the thing was going to be --
I gather Buster didn't have any sort of -- he wasn't an alcoholic or anything like that.
No, nothing like that. Just a nice, easy-going man. Still is.
Where does he live now?
He's in Dallas.
Oh, yeah?
And --
Is he in good health?
Yeah, the last time I heard from him, he was playing piano now. But he was telling me, when he did that movie in '75 with Bruce,* that he was on that, too.
I was just thinking, maybe they ought to get him to do one of these things.
It would be good.
We could cover a period of time. (Unintelligible.)
Yeah, well, now, he can really give you some information. In fact, --
How old is he compared with you?
Well, I don't know, but I imagine that he should be about 71 or 72, somewhere around Basie's age.
Yeah, well, that would be very good because that would be that much ahead of you, wouldn't it?

Yeah, well, there was a man that I gave an interview to last fall, who told me that he had searched and he had found that there were only two guys in that -- I think he said Moten band, the old Southern Serenaders, Walter Page's Blue Devils, that was living. And that Buster Smith was one, but that he couldn't get Buster to --
* Bruce Ricker, producer of Last of the Blue Devils.
Yeah, cause Eddie Barefield (unintelligible) was in the Benny Moten band, but not the -- in the Blue Devils, was he?

The Blue Devils, right. And I forget the -- but he said he tried to get an interview with what's his name, offered to pay him, but he couldn't get very much out of him. And I think he would probably be more willing to talk to you. He talked to me -- now, this was afterwards, and he talked to me and he was telling me about how he was sorry in a way that he didn't come with Basie, that he had -- he's not making that kind of money in the music thing.
Well, I might be able to do it during the winter when I'm in Florida. I can't stand these winters anymore.
I think somebody has already tried to contact him, though.
Well, maybe -- I mean, I don't --
And offered him some money. I think.
I'm just concerned that they should do the right people.

The reason I said it was because there's one man, I think I mentioned to you before, that contacted me about something like this, and he had gone through the whole thing with the Kansas City guys, even Herman Walter and Baby Lovett and --
Of course, Fat Drakes has done a lot
of it.
Well, this seems to be somebody from one of these universities right around here. And he seemed to be --
Somebody got a grant, perhaps.
Yeah, he said he was representing some school up in Massachusetts or New Hampshire or something. But, now, I later found out that -- I think he's from this one down here where Dan Morgenstern is.
Well, did he pay him anything?

He did the first part with me. He gave me fifty dollars. And when he came back, I told him, I said, well, I won't do anything until you let me hear the tapes, because you were supposed to send me the tapes right away. And still didn't send them back so I could hear them.
So when he did finally send them to me, I told him, never mind, I don't want to do it. So --
Well, --
-- he got about maybe 40 minutes, 45 minutes.
When -- you started to say that Buster Smith has really made the Basie band.
Yeah, I'm saying that because, as I said, that Basie band was what we would call in those days a riff band, very little music.
Right.

But they were so well organized, they broadcasted every night, too, at 12:00. And they were so well organized that I remember when Goodman and Hammond and them heard of it, they couldn't believe it, a small band like that sounding so big.

And so these things were all made by head. And you notice that our band was made by head the same way. Now, most of those riffs that we had in our band, Bird or John Jackson, that set them two alto players, (unintelligible). And then Buddy or Piggy set the riffs for the brass.
So you see how we actually were picking up on what Buster was doing in that band. Buster was the one that set those riffs for the --.
Well, I mean, it's really a fact that many of the best arrangements have been heads.
Well, it adds more freedom and the most (unintelligible), it should be the best.
I don't know that --
I don't condemn written music.

I don't think that one should say that they're the best arrangements. What they really are is the thing that -- because they come out of the band, the phrases, fit the guys in the band and they can play them with the maximum feeling and swing, and that -- so the result is --

and, of course, the fact that they're very often blues is something else. I think it's extraordinary how everybody goes around doing these elaborate arrangements and everything, and here comes the blues like "Every Day" or "Diminuendo and Crescendo Blues," with -- that was Duke's biggest hit, after all, it is Paul Gonsalves was playing the blues.
And Johnny Hodges' "Jeep's Blues."
Yeah, that's right.
"After Hours."

That simple blues is it. But, what I wanted to say, when we were describing the jazz and different phases of jazz, like the New Orleans jazz, Chicago jazz, now, a camp meeting - we all look upon Kansas City jazz as like completely imitated from one of those revival meetings, where the preacher and the people are singing, all that living, and there's happenings all around, (unintelligible) and everything. So we always think of Kansas City jazz as something like that, it's something you're bound to feel.

Well, the only another thing I want to take up with you here is that the first time you hear a really good record out of Kansas City, I've heard all those old Benny Moten records and they're pretty corny because they're half New Orleans and --
Yeah, they're a mixture, that's right.
But 1932, when he made Toby and Lafa-
yette," here he has a rhythm section with Basie in it, and these are terrific records, but that is the first time that you hear anything really convincing out of Kansas City.

Now, when they want to say that there is a Kansas City style which was built on riffs, that's okay. It's true, but they cannot put that down purely as a Kansas City invention, because you've got records by the bands in the East with riffs -- Fletcher -- they were all playing riffs.
So, really, I think it's right to say that what was specifically Kansas City was the emphasis on riffs and playing that way.
Right.
Because in the meantime, the East was getting very fancy.

Yeah, and I'm sure of that I'll have to admit that practically all the old bands had the things that they riffed, had riffs on them -- but to give you an example of the Kansas City thing, McShann Max Band, when we'd have our rehearsals, somebody in the reed section, say, we took a stock, say, 720 in the book. (Unintelligible) had this thing, it was one of those things. And we'd find one phrase in there, maybe the reed section would find a phrase in there -- say, well, that man don't swing. So put a so-and-so over there. Put in a star or something over there, and we're going to play it this way to make it sound -- swing more.
Then another thing, like, with the McShann band, I go back to McShann, if you don't mind, McShann built on his band, and his solos, playing behind the beat.
Yeah.

In other words, they always -- he would try to arrange it so that the melodic line or whatever was played just a fraction behind the beat and catch up just before we got to the end of that phrase. That gave it that lazy image, which also meant bluesy sound. If you listen to Hoodie Blues, you'll notice how far behind the real tempo the horns come in, and gave it that real lazy --
Yeah, yeah.
And that, I think, would be more -- they did riff in the East. Now, I give you another comparison, with rhythm sections. The rhythm sections in the East, until very recently was a metronomic beat.
Right.

It didn't accent. But the Western beat was -- (Unintelligible) But most of the time you -- in those days, you'd hear that, if it was an Eastern drummer or Eastern rhythm section, you'd hear that -- just like a metronome, drive you crazy, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick.
Yeah, yeah.
So that, the Western thing gave you a chance to relax, when you heard that backbeat.
Yeah.
Now, that came from the camp meeting from those churches again.

That's why I said, if -- that the rhythm section makes the band. Remember that Basie band, remember, and think of Duke Ellington's band, and you remember how they used to spank a song. In that rhythm section, they were spanking it! They were beating heck out of it. Those horns had to play, I don't care -- I used to say -- in fact, they used to say that you get anybody in Duke Ellington's band, with a rhythm section like that, on you, you'd better play or you're going to jump out of (inaudible) the stand.

Well, what about -- now, one of the things that I wanted to talk to you about, when you're talking of the lazy beat, the behind beat, now, where does the drummer like Cozy Cole, how do you describe what he does?
Well, now, he plays -- while he was in Cab's band, he played a good Eastern beat.
Well, I figured at that time, after he went to Juillard or wherever he went, it seems to me a very big difference.
Yeah, well, now, this might be a physical relapse, because if you'll notice that his foot is in tempo, but his hands can't keep up.
Sometimes it's the other way, with people like Sonny Greer.
Yeah, yeah.
Or with the feet --
His foot got tired.
Yeah.

Now, I noticed this about most of the drummers who have been playing a long time. You don't want to say anything to them, because who am I to tell a drummer how to play. But you sit there playing with a guy, and you see him when he was young, he could do this all day long, on his toes without resting. If he was doing that, he'd have a chance to rest this part of his leg.
But, now, you see a drummer, now he's gotten old and (unintelligible) he's trying to do this. Just think how long your muscles can keep on doing that.
(Unintelligible.) Under here?
Yeah, and you'll see them still doing it, I'm playing on my toes now like I always did. But you're not resting. Them muscles are going to get tired.
Well, I just want -- I don't want to sidetrack, but I'm just interested in the rhythmic thing here. Now, let's just think a minute, well, now, how about a rhythm section like Lunceford's?
Lunceford's was very good. It was --
I don't mean those up-tempo things, when they're doing their sort of two-beat meters.
Yeah. They were very good, and I would
say they were the first movement towards that churchy feeling.
Yeah.
Like, (singing "Mary").
Yeah, that's churchy, too, really.
Yeah, that's churchy, but it's only churchy from what the rhythm section is doing, because the horns were playing in a very unique style, and that was arrangements.
Yeah, yeah.
But it showed that there was relaxation in what they played, like Tommy Dorsey's --
"Yes" / Indeed?
Didn't Dorsey make Remember?
That was Lunceford's band.
No, that was Lunceford's band. Remember, (singing). Dorsey had something just like that.
Well, maybe so.

I don't know whether it was "Remember." was so related. In your sleep you'd still be patting your foot. Anyway, it was something like that. It (unintelligible) those Yeah, those rhythm sections, Lunceford and all those bands that became prominent usually had good swinging rhythm sections.

Yeah. Well, there was another one that I liked, at one time, Claude Hopkins had a nice rhythm section, where he had -- I can't remember the drummer's name, but he was good. Jacobs, I think his name was. That was a very nice,
soft rhythm sound.
Yeah, I remember that coming from the Roseland. I used to hear them -- I didn't know them too well, but they moved.
Yeah.
I'm trying to think of that thing that Don Redman had. Who was it had Cuban Austin or somebody like --
Well, Cuban Austin was in McKinney's Cotton Pickers.
That was the band.
Yeah.
They came out to Kansas City in the Midwest and tore it up. That was --
When was that?

That was, I think, around the time -- but they were just passing through. But -- no, that was before. That was before I got (unintelligible). Yeah, they came all out in Texas and everything. They were supposed to be from Michigan or somewheres.
Yeah. Was Don Redman with them then?
Yeah.
Oh, because that was a good band then.
Yeah, they was spanking them. That's where I got Don and Cuba (unintelligible) associated.
When did you hear Fletcher Henderson?
I only heard him once, and that's right after they made that first after they introduced that great [Israel] little bass player, Crosby, they made "Christopher Columbus."
Oh, you didn't hear him in the -- when he had the good band.
No, I didn't hear them when Hawk was doing that.
Well, I mean, everybody says that it was -- well, Hawk always used to say the records didn't do the band justice, and I'm sure that's true.

Well, I don't think we had a chance to hear them too much on the air. I might have heard him, but I don't have anything that reminds me of Fletcher. I think I saw him once or twice in Kansas City. But, somehow, I wasn't just -- probably so prejudiced in favor of Kansas City bands. Maybe it was that. Because I know they had played Kansas City at night when they had the jam sessions.
Well, there wasn't quite -- what we're really talking about with Kansas City, is a sort of looseness, really, isn't it?
Right, right.
I mean, that's when Basie first came. That was what -- I mean, this is --
The front line wasn't that much as far as -- I mean, the unified front line wasn't that much as far
as Basie was concerned.
No. But --
But how they all --

In a way, -- now, for instance, Columbia is issuing all of Lester Young's records, re-issuing all of Lester Young's records. Well, I think, just as you say, that Jay McShann is heard, by the emphasis on Charlie Parker. I think Basie should be heard.
Yeah.
All these records are coming out under Lester's name. I don't --
Is that what they're doing?
More or less, yeah. It's the Lester Young collection. It's going to be all the records with Basie. I don't think that's right. They should have done it through a complete Count Basie collection.
Yeah.
This is -- John Hammond is responsible for that, and he's a big --
And he's a big friend of Basie's.
I can't understand that.
And you know something? I worked with Prez for so long at Birdland, and --
Yeah, it's nearly done.
And --
Well, it gets to the end, though. I could put it on the speed and take it out. But it doesn't -- at the end, it won't run as fast as it will just playing.
Well, what I wanted to say, I better wait until it's the end.
Yeah, hold your thought. (End of Side One.)

Well, now, this was -- and Prez never got over it, never got over it. And when that man would come down to Birdland, he'd sit down there with a smile on his face and say (inaudible). And Prez, rather than using curse words, he called everybody Tommy Tucker. And he said to Joe and I, he said, Lady Ramey and Lady Jones -- he called everybody Lady, and he'd say, Tommy Tucker's in the house.
Tommy Tucker?
Yeah. Which meant -- (laughter) Tommy Tucker's in the house.
I mean, why did he get Prez fired, then?

It seems that Prez wanted $125, and he told Basie that he wasn't worth it, or something like that. The way Prez used to tell me, -- as I said before, as close as Prez and I were, and I was the best man at his wedding and like the father of his children there for a long time, he used to tell me these things. And it was on many occasions when John Hammond really made efforts to try to get friendship, regain
his friendship. He never did, never did.
Well, the circumstances -- what was the story, though, that he got Billie Holiday and Audrey fired?
I never knew about it, but I knew, first of all, that Preston and Billie were very close.
Yeah.
And whenever they would get together and talk, that's all they'd talk about, about John. And how that band was on its way to make it and -- oh, they just tore it asunder.
You know, we were talking awhile ago about -- they're putting these records out in the name of --
Lester Young.
Lester Young.
Yeah.

And how insulting it should be to Basie. But it might have been that in those days, because like overnight, Billie Holiday and Preston was springing ahead, high, so fast. And in fact when people were going to buy Basie's records, they'd hear Lady Day or go and buy records to hear Lester Young, like that. Did you hear Lady Day sing so-and-so? If you heard anything else, it would have been (inaudible). Young.
Now, it might have been in there but to preserve Basie's back in those days.
Well, why did he get Claude Williams

Yeah. But, remember, as I said before, they picked up Claude Williams -- I don't know, he'd been with Benny Moten, I think. But, anyway, they got him at the last minute, and put him in the band when they got ready -- enlarged the band. And we all knew Claude was very, very temperamental.
Oh, well, there was some reason for that.
Yeah, it probably was that. It might have been that he wanted more solos, because he was very demanding, like that.
And Tabby Smith -- wasn't there something wrong with him?

Tabby Smith had -- all of them in those days, those trumpet players and saxophone players were always filing their mouthpieces. And it was a possibility of them getting brass that they shaved off into their lips.
Yeah.
And getting -- well, Tabby's lips started going bad on him.
Oh. Now, there would be a reason then why possibly he went, but Joe Jones told me that Joe Keyes was a marvelous musician.
You know what? Any band that went to the Apollo Theatre, they would go find Joe Keyes and hire
him to play that first thing and carry that band through. He played those shows, play the man's arrangements just like he had been playing in the band forever.
Well, --
His was an alcoholic situation.
He was an alcoholic?
Yeah.
Well, that was why John got rid of him then.
I imagine, I imagine.
Because he used to be very --

Some people say it was because he had a strong purse, but he had a thin tone. And I always thought he had a good enough tone as a lead. The guys would play those high notes, they'd usually get a thin tone. Look at how great Cat Anderson was, or is, and his tone had to get thin when he started playing them high notes.

But it's like Coleman Hawkins always was critical of Russell Smith. He always said Fletcher (unintelligible) But everybody else always says that Russell Smith was a great lead trumpet. But Hawk always criticized him, and I think that was the reason. But that was the -- it was accurate and everything, but it was a thin sound.
It could have been. But in the case with Basie's band, the remnants of the Kansas City thing was slowly
being taken away. That was what most of the guys were saying, the looseness, but the fact that he had such a powerful rhythm section --
Yeah.
-- held that thing together, regardless. And the same thing to go back, like, with Duke. But, now, if you --
Well, I mean, would you say Duke had a powerful rhythm section?
Oh, amazing. Amazing. He had the -- what was the old man you was talking about the other day?
Wellman Braud
Braud, and Sonny Greer, good God, good God. And Duke and that guitar player, what was his name?
Freddy Guy
Guy, oh, my goodness.
Yeah, well, I --
And this was -- I remember when that 'Ring Them Bells' came out.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
And I was a little -- just beginning in Austin, and --
See, that was a totally different kind of rhythm section.
That was the first time we heard -- you
could hear that bass player coming through. You could see how they were teaming.
Yeah.
Sonny Greer knew back in those days how to team with that bass --
Yeah.
-- fiddle, because it wasn't as strong and couldn't cut through like that bass horn had been doing. And I think that changed Duke's whole atmosphere around, when he got --

Well, the other one -- since you're talking about it and we didn't mention, I guess you must have had the records in those days, was the one with Louis Russell and Paul Barbarin and Pops Foster Constan.
Yeah, yeah.
Now, those records made played in 1928, but, I mean, that was a very powerful --
Rhythm section, yeah.
And it's very close to what you get four years later on Benny Moten's records. It's almost the same sort of sound.
Yeah.
So that came out of Kansas City -- out of New Orleans.
New Orleans, yeah.
Like all your old .
That showed that they were getting away from that heavy foot.
That's right.
And getting their teamwork together.
That's -- of course, that wasn't like the four-four that you're going to get out of Kansas City.
No, but it was sensible enough where you could appreciate what the whole rhythm section --
Right, right.
Now, you think back in the days, like Baby Dodds and them, they were the guys that was driving that front line with those horns and things, you know.
Yeah.
If you heard the piano, he was tinkling in there, and the bass horn was just going boom-te-boom, and those things. But, still, they swung in those days.

They swung, all right. I mean, though, the thing is that until Earl came along with that style of -- that stride style of Fats and James P. Johnson was fine in the solo, but it didn't really go with the bass drums, did it?
No. And you have to say that Earl definitely was the father of making a solo pianist being heard and appreciated in a big band.
Yeah, that's right.
And before that time, that piano was completely in the background.

Well, when you three got together Jay McShann and jointly shared that Gus, now, what were you -- what were you thinking in terms of, I mean, had you heard -- I mean, were you doing your own thing or were you influenced by Basie, or what?
We were slightly influenced by Basie, and I definitely was influenced by Walter Page.
Yeah.

But we used to have our conferences and talk, and I would express to them what Page had told me, about how we could should team, how that bass drum drummer's foot shouldn't be too heavy, and how the bass player should stay away from trying to run every chord that goes along, but get a straight line where you can push, and Max McShann was naturally talented in how to play with the band, anyway.

We began to find each other, and it was during our first year that lots of times the horns would lay out -- McShann had the horns lay out and the rhythm section and would just walk for maybe five or ten minutes. Just McShann cooking on the piano and --
When did you get the guitar player?
Sometime in late '41, something like that. Now, we had him in 1940, but I don't think he made the
records with us.
Didn't you need him, or was that just sort of --
I think that was a fill-up. Back in those days, certain halls had to have a certain number of musicians. And I think it was a fill-up, because --
And that's sort of appearance, too, I mean, people are accustomed to seeing a guitar there. I guess if you hadn't got one, they'd think you were --
Yeah, immature, incorrect band or something. But --
But, Gene, one thing, since we're talking about McShann's records, as a result of these -- the popularity of these blues records, you never got to record all the bands' arrangements, did you?
Only one, that was Scottie's band thing, (unintelligible) "Swingmatism."
Yeah. Well, Jay told me that when he was inducted off the bandstand, that night the book was stolen.
Yeah, and for a long time, Johnny thought and I think he told Jay that he thought I took the thing. I'll tell you what happened there.
First of all, when McShann first -- well, when he had to leave we played the Howard Theatre in Washington, and this was in January of '44, and we had -- the band was booked

in the Plantation Club in California. When McShann had to leave for his pre-induction thing, whatever that was, and so he put the band in my charge and I took the band on one-nighters all the way across -- that's when -- the story -- when I told the story about Bird getting beat up by the cops in Jackson, Mississippi? You didn't hear that?

We played at a -- it was a new dance hall right on the river. And there was a curfew for blacks. Had to be in the house with the lights out by 11:00. And now, it was down at this place -- everybody was still talking about that place where somebody set that dance hall on fire and burned up all those musicians.
Natchez.

Natchez, Mississippi. Now, this was right on the river, like that. We had two valets, so we got there and got the instructions, and I told all the guys. I said, well, we're going to put one of you on the door to check the take, and we want another guy to stand outside and watch for anybody that's coming, because this was a brand-new, unpainted dance hall, right on the river, there.

And so we want you to watch them because we know how mean these people are in Mississippi. So they said -- it was quite a few white guys that you could see standing back there, but nothing ever happened. We played the thing, we
got through, we got home, we got into bed and turned out the lights, all of us except Walter Brown and Bird.

Now, they didn't have a light on the front porch where they slept. This was a rooming house. And so naturally all of us in the band filled that house up and so Bird and what's his name -- the lady gave them a bed on the front porch. Now, I don't know whether they were smoking pot or cigarettes. Evidently they must have been smoking cigarettes because if it had been pot they probably would have been in jail forever.

But, anyway, from what we got -- I had to call Johnny Tuning and he had to come and get Bird out, we didn't know where Bird was. Til finally the lady came, the lady that owned the place, and she stayed next door because we had taken her bedroom, too. And she said, the cops came last night and took two of your boys away.

And so we found out that the cops had said that the guys had a light on the front porch. They were supposed to have been laying in bed, smoking cigarettes. Because it was a screened porch. So they took Bird and what's his name. We got them two days later. I was in Little Rock, Arkansas. We had played Memphis and Nashville, the band was in Little Rock when they caught up with us. Johnny had to go get them and bring them to catch up with us.
And Bird -- and they had knots on their head big enough to hang a hat on.
Had beaten them up?
Oh, they really had a beating. And so I carried the band on to --
Why in the hell would they do that? Or do you think Bird sort of sassed them?

No, no, you didn't have to do anything. In fact, Bird was gifted, he got us out of trouble many a time. I remember one time, we were on our way to New Orleans and we got just past -- gotten just through Baton Rouge, and the cops caught us and said, 'You Yankee niggers, huh?' And Bird got up and no, sir, yes, sir and everything, turned him out nice and his clothes fit on him, and how his father worked down here in Louisiana. His father had never even been there. And after all he said, they actually escorted us to the next town.

Bird was talented at that. I'm pretty sure it wasn't that. It just was some people to use as examples, like, in Texas they used to do that back in the -- when we were kids, get some guy and lynch him and drag him through the black neighborhood or something.
Oh, yeah.
Tar him or something, put something on him and drag him through the neighborhood, as an example to put fear in the rest of the --
Just to keep them frightened.
Keep frightened, yeah. So I think it

was something like that. Anyway, there was no case of -- Johnny had to pay $25 each for them. But we got to Los Angeles and it was there that McShann joined us. And we played the Plantation Club and then McShann had to go back to the Army. Now, he's inducted into the Army.
You told me he was inducted right after Stan, in --
Yeah, well, what had happened, he had been inducted but they gave him permission to come back.
Oh, I see.
And play that one night.
Yeah, yeah.

But it seemed like they gave him a curfew of -- since they had had so much trouble getting him -- since he was always begging excuses, carry my band a little further or something. And so I got the band, I remember we got to Amarillo, Texas, and when they found out McShann wasn't going to be there, they cancelled the dance.

And I went around and got some of what you'd call the thugs, the regular guys that played, so the man said he would get us the ballroom free if we could get -- give the dance ourselves. So we gave the dance ourselves, 50 cents a head, just to get us enough money to make it on into Kansas City.
And we got to Kansas City and Jay was there wating

for us.

And it was understood --
Well, didn't you have a piano player?
Yeah, we had Skip Hall. No, we didn't have Skip Hall, we -- I think we had Bob Merrill playing the piano then, because Bob had come back from Earl Hines. Yeah.
Bob who?
Bob Merrill. He was banging on the piano.
Oh.
Yeah, because Skip had gone into the service then.
Yeah.
And so, --
Well, when Skip Hall was around that band, did he play piano?
Sometimes McShean would walk off and Skip was glad to get over there and play.
But did he travel with you as an arranger then?

Yeah, he would travel as an arranger and kind of help with the transportation and sometimes on the door and like that. But McShean had -- we had made an agreement with Johnny -- in fact, they wanted to put it in writing and I should have got them to do it then, that I was supposed
to take over the band and it would still be Jay McShann and his band, featuring Walter Brown, under the direction of Gene Ramey.
Yeah.

Well, as soon as they took Jay off of that bandstand, Johnny Tunno and somebody from that office, RKO or Rockwell (unintelligible) who it was, O'Keefe or who it was, they came and said, well, listen, we have decided that we're taking too much of a chance in doing it this way, until Jay gets back this is going to be Walter Brown and his band, under the direction of Gene Ramey.

So I told them, I said, under those circumstances, you'll have Walter Brown and his band, because Gene Ramey is not going. I said, I'm sorry I got to give you this on a short notice, because we were supposed to be in Cincinnati the next night. I said, I'm sorry to tell you that I am not going.

Now, when I told them that, I told them in front of all the guys and all the guys got mad, too, because nobody wanted to work under Walter Brown, he was a far worse dope addict than Bird was. Very hard to get along with. And you give him complete control of that band, --
Well, it was ridiculous, wasn't it?
Yeah. So I said, no, I'm not going to make it. So, now, naturally, McShann didn't know and Johnny, --
he didn't know what happened. I told him I wasn't going, and I even left my bass down in the Municipal Auditorium there in Kansas City, and didn't go back til the next morning at 10:00 to pick it up.
And when I came to pick it up, there wasn't nothing there and the guys evidently had gotten on a train and gone. Now, it could have been somebody there in the place, because nobody liked it.
No, well, Jay said that two guys came in and saw the caretaker at the auditorium and told them they were to pick up McShann's things and went off with a trunk full of music.
That might have been two of the guys in the band.
Two of the guys in the band?
Might have been. And I still got my ideas of who they might have been, but, now, you think -- once before, when we had 'Lucky' Ennis as a guitar player, --
Yeah.

-- in charge of getting the luggage home, and the band -- we had gone back into New York City and was at the Woodside Hotel, when this guy came in and he said, man, all the music was stolen down in Baltimore. We had just finished that theater in Baltimore.
And I had to get on a train and go back down there,
and the stuff was still sitting in the back at that theatre, where he had never sent it off to the railroad station. And it was shortly after that -- now, this was in late '42.
It was Lucky --
Lucky Enos, he was supposed to be in charge of the handling of the --
Yeah, he was supposed to put the music on -- yeah, I got you.

Yeah, he was supposed to have taken it down there and put it on the railroad train. And had it shipped into New York. And evidently he was out balling some chick or something and they locked up the theater, so he came on home and said, the music -- I don't know where the music is. So I had to get on a train and go back down there, and got it.
Well, --

But, anyway, McShann -- I mean, they -- for a long time they kept writing me and saying, well, what did you do to the music? Now, I was still in Kansas City. I was working at the new Reno club, out on Independence, with Oliver Todd and some other guys.

And I finally convinced them, I said, well, if I had the music, it had to be around here because I got no other place to go. So they finally got up off me. Then I did have a chance to talk with McShann and he was convinced that I
wouldn't do it no way. No, well, I mean, if you -- I mean, anybody that would take that music, you would have thought, would have used it.
Yeah. The (unintelligible) there had to sell by copies, but --
But the thing is, now, when you go East, we haven't talked about that, when you go East with McShann to play at the Savoy Ballroom, opposite Lucky Millinder, what happened there?

Well, we had gotten a telegram and McShann doesn't even remember this. But Johnny Tunno brought us a telegram and I had that in my scrapbook for a long time, and I gave it to Johnny after we got to New York, and I never got it back. And the same way with those pictures that you have of the pre-McShann band? I was the only one that kept a scrapbook. I had everything that happened.
Who did you give them to?
Johnny Tunno, who was the boss of the band.
Oh, oh, oh, oh, oh.
And I never got it back. But --
He was in New York then, was he?
No, he was still travelling with us.
Oh.

And, man, he really sacrificed for this band. A lot of time he and his family would go hungry, Bird or somebody of them would come and get his last dollar or something, or come get money from his wife.
And he's so anxious to keep the band happy and everything. His wife and all of them would --
He was a good guy.
Oh, yeah, still is. And so, Lucky sent this telgram, we're going to send you hicks back to the sticks. Not a telegram, it was one of those one-cent postcards. And so --
What did he say?
'Going to send you hicks right back to the sticks.'
I'll send you hicks --
'We're going to send you hicks back to the sticks.'
Oh. Was that supposed to be a joke?

Yeah, you know, in other words, they're going to blow us out. So, man, we started getting ready. Now, the way I have it is that we opened on February 13, Friday, February 13, 1942. I think MeShan had it 1941. I know --
No, it's '42, I've got that -- I've got it's '42, yeah.
Yeah. And so we opened, first of all,

McShann had a new Buick -- not a new Buick, he had a pretty good Buick, one of those big old long Buicks. He had five or six guys in the band. But I was driving. Never having been on the Pennsylvania Turnpike in Pennsylvania before, I saw that route -- I think it was 24, it looked like it was the shortest route to New York.

But what I didn't know was that it was up and over the mountains, instead of taking the turnpike that goes around and through. And, man, we struggled and we struggled and we got into New York. I told McShann, I said, you know what? I said, we get this -- when I make my first $1,000 I'm going to buy you a new Buick.

And we were always just buddies -- just like, you know, break bread on anything. And we got into New York, dragging and tired and everything. We got up there on the bandstand, the people were looking at us like we were nothing, because Lucky was on the main bandstand, we were on that side where the Savoy Sultans used to play.
Yeah, yeah.

And we hit that first note and when Lucky Mullinder came in and his cats didn't want to go over to that bandstand. They didn't get on that stand, they were over standing in front of us, man, what's your name? Yeah? We had them already -- Panama was in that band.
Now, what had happened, the Savoy Sultans, the middle

1940's, the Savoy Sultans and their band, and Coleman Hawkins had a big band, came out there on tour and they battled us in Kansas City. And we tore them up. And they had already gone back to New York and telling the cats, watch out for that band.
Well, now, I've read that the McSharry band arrived in New York, a raggedy band with raggedy sound. Were the uniforms beaten up or anything?
Well, we had a blue coat and brown pants.
I mean, the photographs of the band on the stand looked quite sharp.
Yeah, well, now, that was the uniform we had.
Yeah.
But we had cardboard stands, we had -- bought the music -- like, the metal music racks?
Yeah.
And the guys went and got derbies and had them pinned on, you know. In other words, the stuff -- everything we had was so shabby looking, and we only had that one uniform, you know.
Yeah.
And we all -- at that time every guy in that band would get soaking wet, because we would --
Sweat.
Sweat, yeah. From the time we hit that first note until the time we got off that bandstand, we didn't let up.
Well, Lucky Millinder and the band was a good band though, wasn't it?
Wow, we'd been listening to that blue ribbon band from all over the country and they were cooking like mad.
Yeah.
So that night, we heated it so hot for Lucky Millinder that he got up on top of the piano and directed the band there and jumped off and almost broke his leg.

But I think it was the next year that -- yeah, I think it was the next year, '43, that -- Andy Gibson told me that that was the year when that was the great band of Lucky Millinder's, he said he wrote a lot of arrangements for them and he got a strong band, and this was another casualty that -- just as you can't hear Parker and (unintelligible) Dizzy with Earl you can't hear Lucky Miller with this band, the following year.
Well, now, I do remember -- I think it was about '43 when they got George Durivier, and they probably still had Panama in the band.
Yeah, yeah.
And -- but Lucky always -- of the Joe Glaser bands, Lucky was the only one that was really paying

those guys. Andy Kirk -- they had Andy Kirk or Erskine Hawkins and all those guys, paying them 40 dollars a week. And them guys was suffering. So Lucky always managed to get some cats and good arrangements.
Yeah, well, that -- so, actually, I guess that when they saw you in these beaten up uniforms with these stands, they figured that they had nothing to fear.
Yeah, and --

Johnny said that when they started going in the books, these guys began to get restless and then he called for a number called 'Roll 'Em,' and he said you played it for about 30 minutes, and went into -- do you remember that?
I remember playing a blues. I didn't know whether it was Roll 'Em or what.
Well, he said it was called Roll 'Em, and he said they went -- they were ten minutes into Lucky's time and he said after that Lucky finally sat in with these guys.
(Laughter.)
It's an exaggeration, but it's a good story.
Well, that could be. I remember, Lucky was -- he started changing men right away.
Yeah. Well, he always did, because I think it was Dizzy who said -- no, somebody told me that Lucky fired himself one night. He made a flop and by the time the
time the notice was nearly up, he'd come and (unintelligible). give him ten dollars more to stay.
(Changed my mind here)
Yeah, I (unintelligible), man, come on, let's have a drink. But --
Yeah.

-- now, that was on a Friday. That Sunday, the first Sunday there at the Savoy, we had to do a matinee which started about 4:00. And so in 15 minutes, we only played two tunes. I think we played something like 'Moten Swing' or something, and then we played 'Cherokee.' And, now, Bird started blowing -- this was up there, as fast as anything Max Roach ever played. I think we were the first band to ever play that extremely fast tempo.
But, anyway, we had it way up there, and --
On 'Well, "Cherokee"?'
On 'Cherokee', yeah.
Yeah.

And somebody from the head office in the studio called that man on the -- that had the earset on, and told him, says, let them go ahead, don't stop them, let them play. And we played 45 minutes more, just the rhythm section and Bird, with the horn setting the riffs from time to time.
On 'Cherokee.'
On 'Cherokee.' Now, everybody heard this, like, all the guys, the musicians and everybody was -- they
didn't have to go to work until eight that night and they all had tuned in on this thing. And --
Oh, this was on the radio?
This was on the radio.
Oh.
And everybody heard it. So that night, you couldn't get close to the bandstand for musicians. Everybody, man, who was that band? You hear that saxophone player? Who was that?
Well, when it came to beating Millender in this battle, I take it that that was really the band, --
