What did you fight about then?

He came after me. What had happened, we were in Boston in the Tick Tock Club, and now, we were working under the supervision of Don Redman. So we played a tune -- it was kind of difficult. And -- for a first trumpet player, you know -- and so I was in charge of the band and the music and what's his name was just -- Don Redman was just fronting, you know.

So Bob is supposed to have torn up a piece of music, you know. So right away Gus comes and tells me. And I look up. I'm in a dressing room, you know, and I look up, and then Bob come in and says, 'Well, what are you going to do about it,'

so and so, and he had a picture, about to hit me, you know, and I cut him, and somehow I stopped that picture and got my knife. From that day on I never carried a knife, you know, because I don't even know -- I don't know anything else about it, you know, just that quick, you know.
And then I was so ashamed and disgusted with myself for having been led into something like that, that I just quit the band.
Well, did you hurt him much?
He was cut from the -- right in front of his ear all the way down to his chin, you know, and --
It is really the danger of carrying a knife.
Yeah, you know, you --
It's like carrying a gun.
Yeah, you go for it. You go for it on the least little thing. When you don't have it, you going to find another way out, you know.
Well, I mean, you know, you -- everybody loses his temper some time or other, and if you're carrying something like that --
You're tempted to use it.
-- you're liable to go for it.
Yeah.
It's a mistake.
So I --

I always remember, you know, Cat Anderson blowing in Tizol's ear, thought Tizol was playing around and he kept blowing the notes in his ear, and Tizol whipped out his knife. This was when they were recording with Basie. And everybody thought it was very funny. Of course, it could have been dangerous.

Yeah. Yeah, you know, that's a hurting thing for somebody to do that in your ear anyway, you know. It seems like he's asking for something. Well, it was the same thing, you know. See, I made a contract with McShann when I didn't go with -- with --
Charlie Barnet.

Charlie Barnet. So -- and having won that citation, you know, for -- DownBeat thing -- and then every time they had a show or something, every band that came in town, Jay and I and Johnny Tumino would have to go out there for me to play with this band -- Woody Herman, Tommy Dorsey, every band that came out to Fairyland, I had to get up there and play with them.
It was sort of publicity for you too.

Yeah, to show me off, one of those things, McShann's band, one of those things, you know. It began -- it became a thing -- McShann says he knew it all the time, but he just didn't want to say anything to me, but
those guys really hated my guts. Now, these are the same guys that I helped to get into the band, you know. But --
Oh, I see. They resented you -- resented you.

Yeah, that position. That's why -- in those -- I went to 52nd Street, I refused to take any solos. For a long time a guy who said, 'Take a solo,' I said, 'No, I'm in the rhythm section.' I thought that maybe I could -- would be in a peaceful manner rather than that, because before that I used to catch Pettiford and tear him up, you know?
Really?
Oh, he got so he wouldn't even look for me.
(Laughter)
Oh?

He'd see me coming. I went in the Spotlight like last time I did that was right after I went on 52nd Street. He kept on egging me on, you know, because I used to catch him out in the Middle West and tear him up, you know. So he -- he had gotten a name because he made that good record with Hawk, you know, and he was playing the spotlight. He kept on saying, 'Man, you can't play.' He said, I'm going to get you. He said, 'You ain't -- you ain't no bass player.' So I went up there and played. Al Hall remembers that. I went up there and played on him, and I tore him up so

bad, he got drunk and couldn't play anymore. I had to go finish the night for him. So anyway, after that now, he kept soloing and on I didn't. So when I became the house man at Birdland, Joe Jones and I, every night that Pettiford could, he'd come down there with his bass, and he'd go on that side of the bandstand, and I'd take my bass and go right off, you know.
And he said, man, what's the matter? You chicken? I said, no, I just want you to know I don't solo no more. I stopped it altogether. But anyway --
Did you really? Did you really sort of get out of the way of soloing because of that?

Yeah, well, that stayed on my mind. In fact, it's on my mind a lots now, you know. I just -- you know, I said, I think I'll be able to get along better in the band if I, first of all, don't have anything to do with management, you know, don't be so tight with the --
Oh, that I can see.

Yeah. And the other thing is taking solos, because, see, every tune before Bird came in regularly, I had a solo on every tune, even when they're dancing and I used to tell McShann. I said, 'Listen, the people are dancing, you know. This is no time for a bass solo.' He said, 'Go on and play a walk-on solo because the cats, everybody dig you, you know.' And for him, I'd go on and do it. But --

You know, I always used to think -- I mean I'm not -- I think that the bass solo did get out of hand, you know, when -- you know when Roy and Hawk used to be in the Metropole, every number has to have a bass solo. It doesn't make sense.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Well, every number -- I was at the Hickory House with Duke once. I can't remember who was there, but, you know, one of these pianists (inaudible). Every we had dinner number has a bass chorus, you know, and (inaudible) there, and you know, it wasn't any dazzling bass solo. Duke said -- (inaudible), like commercials on TV, you know, because bass solo --
It's not that much variety you can do with a bass solo.
Also you mustn't forget that very often you can't really hear, you know.
No. You don't get the whole essence.
No, in a place like that with clatters of noise and waiters hollering, to follow a bass solo is not easy.

Yeah, I've always hated it. I used to -- I said, not more than two bass solos a night is enough for a bass player, you know, if at all. Walter Page didn't take any solos at all, you know, and except walking, you know, the
walking solos with the rhythm section, but I had to establish that thing, and the bosses and everything wanted me to take solos, you know.
So under what circumstances did you come back?
To Max Roach? McShann?
Yeah.

Well, he -- he kept on calling me to come back, you know. And I joined him in Chicago. It was -- no -- there was no peaceful agreement or anything, you know, just -- he said, well, come on back, he says. You just had a fight, and Bob is still here, and he knows that he intimidated you, you know. He started the fight. So you fought back in self defense.

In fact, everybody thought the cops was going to arrest me. The cops came up there and told me, said, 'You go on home.' One night there was an emcee, a white man from New Orleans. And he went over to the cops and told him, said, 'If it had been me, I'd have killed that man.' He said, 'This guy had his back turned, and he looked and this guy had a glass pitcher, fixing to hit him on the back of the head.'
Oh, so -- might have killed you.
Yeah. And he said, if -- if it hadn't -- Bo McKenny's the one that told me, said, look out. And I looked around, and I just happened to see that pitcher coming
down, and somehow I got my arm up, and somehow I got my knife, you know.
Was he drunk?
He had been drinking, but it was just that he had some -- a stew going, you know, he had some --
So then you were back with McShann until the time he went --
Until he went in the service.
And then after that, when they wanted to make Walter Brown the leader, you --
I gave it up.
The band collapses then, does it?

Well, I understand six men got to Cincinnati, no music or nothing, you know. And that's the last I -- that you can say that happened to that band. But by that time McShann didn't hardly -- they only had Schoolboy and John Jackson of the -- of the what's his name in -- Kansas City musicians in the band. By that time they had gotten in from Detroit, Ohio, Washington, D. C., somebody of Ernie Fields' out band, it was just, you know, wasn't Kansas City at all.
No.
But I stayed in Kansas City, and I worked six weeks with --
Did Gus Johnson remain with the band
No, Gus went in the service the week of Thanksgiving in '43.
Oh, that's right. He went in the Navy, didn't he?
I don't know whether it was the Navy or the Army.
Oh, I --

But he left us, and we got a guy out of Dayton, Ohio. He was also kind of hooked on that stuff. So that -- Walter turned around and found himself another buddy to -- and that's when John Jackson and Schoolboy and a whole lots of these young, new musicians started to get --
How -- how much was Bird's sort of addiction showing in these McCann years. Was it --

Well, it wasn't that same way it was doing to Jackknife, scratching his chin, you know, scratching his face, which is always an obvious sign, you know. It wasn't that. In fact, it's very rarely you would see him doing the way, he was standing there nodding and that sort of thing.
But you could tell. And -- I mean was he -- did he generally remain sort of in good control or not?
Generally speaking, Bird would be in

control, and the other guys who were trying to be like him and using it, were the ones that was slouching in other words, it was stopped you, you know. But then, see, Bird was wise enough, you know. They had -- back in Kansas City, while we were playing in Kansas City at a place called Tootie's Mayfair, Bird had gotten all the guys that was following him to take nutmeg, take a teaspoon of nutmeg, you know. That's a different kind of high from -- from the drug thing.

Then when they got to New York, they found some -- oh, then by that time he was hanging out with Dameron at the Tadd Dameron, and they were experimenting with everything. They had some -- they would even soak the reed of their mouthpiece in benzedrine water, you know.
(Laughter)
Now, this was a way -- a waker-upper. And the drug is a go-to-sleeper, you know.
Now, did that not make things worse, though?
Well, it made things different, you know.
I mean did you try it?
No, I never took it. I never touched anything.
I wonder -- you know, I couldn't -- I always remember in England, when you'd have custard pies
with nutmeg sprinkled all over it. I'd never -- I suppose, though, if you took a teaspoonful of it --

Yeah, you see what they did, when they'd take a teaspoonful of it and then take a drink of water, it gets down in some nick in your intestines, and after it lays there -- you won't get high that same day. But the next day or maybe the next three days you're walking like a sick duck or something, you know.
Really? Well, I'll be darned.

And the only way we found it out was a man that Tootie had a fine dinner service, and he, you know, he needed this -- he'd go down to the store and buy nutmeg just to have it, buy supplies anyway, and the man out of the grocery store said, 'You sure must be cooking lots of cakes and pies.' And he said, why? And he said, you get some of the colored guys coming down here," he said, "they buying up all my nutmeg."
(Laughter and simultaneous remarks)
-- really funny, aren't they?
But we've got to -- we've got to sort of move it a little bit now. After this -- after McShane's -- you're finished with McShane. Now what do you do?
Well, I stayed there six weeks with -- at the Reno Club with that old man (inaudible) that had that other Reno. They made him move out of there, and they tore
it down and built a courthouse or something there. So he bought a place out there on Independence, going towards the Truman's home, out that direction. I worked out there for six weeks and --
: Who with?

Todd and some different guys. It wasn't a leader. It was just about four or five guys working there. I can't remember all the guys. But anyway, and Luis Russell came through. He had lost his bass player, who was Ted Sturgis, you know. I don't know who he went with, but Ted left with somebody, so they asked me at the last moment if I would go with them. I said, 'Well, I can't go tonight.' So the cat said, 'Well, we'll take off. We'll cancel our St. Louis job if you'll go with us. We'll put it back.' So I told them, all right, I'd go, see. I went with them, had -- Lil Green was singing.
: Oh, with Lil Green?
And we had Razz Mitchell on drums there. He was with what's his name, Luis Russell, so we had a swinging rhythm section.
: Well, what year was this?
This was '44.
: '44. Oh, I didn't know about this Luis Russell band.
Well, this was a band he put together
and -- Oh, more or less to accompany Lil Green?
Yeah, I guess so.
I see. I've got you.

And because most of the guys he had in there were -- few were pure amateurs with the exception of Holmes and another alto player that had been -- I think he went blind or something. Then he had -- kept Jesse Powell, who was a beginner, learner. He didn't even know how to take a solo, couldn't play 12 bars without getting lost and all that sort of thing.
He had -- he didn't have any horns. They had some guys that could read, but they couldn't solo at all.
I see. Yeah.
So anyway, I stayed with them. We did -- we had -- also had Gatemouth Moore, who later quit and became a pastor down in Memphis, and he turned out to be a great blues singer.
Yeah.
And so with Lil Green and Gatemouth there, and then we had -- the Inkspots were with us on a couple of tours and Ella --
Package.
Yeah, most of the time they billed us

with a package, you know, because everybody was -- they were all working out of [Moe] Gale's office, you know. So we -- we went in the Apollo three times, and we went -- time I was with him. I left him in October.
You weren't in the band when she had a fellow called Howard Calendar conducting it?
Yes, he was going with him and he was playing trumpet in the band.
Were you in the band then?
Yeah.
Well, after I picture --
No.
-- pictured that band, I must ask you if you know them.
Well, I may not have been there.
Well, you might know some of them.

The guy that took my place was -- well, first there's a guy from Galveston, Texas, named Barney Richmond, and then another guy from New York named Thomas (inaudible). So I might not have been in the band.
Well, I bet you know some of them, though, but --
I'm sure I know --
I met Howard Calendar somewhere. I'd never heard of him, you know, and he gave me this picture.
I don't know any of the people.
Yeah, well, they had no business and up as being in that sort of a jazz band. They were marching band style musicians, you know.
(Laughter)
Well, listen. We're running into our last half hour. When do you get to New York and the association with Prez Prez?

Well, I -- first of all, I got into Lips -- saw Lips, and he told me, said, 'Why don't you stay in town?' I said, 'Well, I want to, but I can't get nothing down on 52nd Street.' He said, 'Well, that's a clique,' but he said, 'I'll get you in two nights a week with me.'
Lips Page?

Lips Page, yeah. So he said, 'Well, go ahead and quit.' So I quit. And he got me on down there, and now, I had to apply for my union thing, and that union law was I couldn't play with any out of town musicians. I had to give up playing with anybody, you know, like guys who didn't have #802 cards.
So I had a six months' probation on that. So I --
Oh, to get in the union?
Yeah. So up until that six months I couldn't work steady on any job, but I was -- Lips was getting giving me plenty of work. He and I worked with Ike Quebec Ike Cree
back in the
Oh, you were coming -- because when you're coming in with a traveling band, that was okay.
Yeah.
Yeah, I --

I had to pay ten percent. It was all right. But now, when I joined, then I had to -- I couldn't work with any traveling musicians then. I had to work with only 802 musicians six months. And so -- and a guy named Morris that played drums with, I think -- what's the guy that had the band down at the Horseshoe? He was a drummer with -- down at the Diamond Horseshoe for a long time.
Morris, I don't know a Morris.
I don't know.
He wasn't a great drummer. He played in that society band. What was the colored guy that had the band down at the Diamond Horseshoe?
I don't know.
Black --
Sisler -- Noble Sissle?
Noble Sissle, yeah.
Oh, yeah?
And so this guy got a job up playing in the Bronx, and so I did three nights with him and two nights with Lips down on 52nd Street, and that was enough to carry me

through. Now McShann gets out of the Army. Naturally, and I've got to go six months before I can work with out of town musicians. So Barry Ulanov and several of them come over there almost threatening me, you know, said, 'Look, you got to go back with McShann. He needs you, and you need him because you cannot make it in New York.'

So I told them, I said, 'Well, look, man, I am trying to get my #802 card, and I can't play with McShann because he's an out of town musician.' So I explained to McShann. He understood. And then I got situated then, and I went on in to working with Ben Webster steady. Then I went over to Tiny Grimes, who's an evil man if there ever was one, an evil man.
We went over and --
Was what then?
Was an evil man.
Evil?
Tiny Grimes.
Evil?
(Side Two)
In 1949 Teddy Reig wanted you to form a trio?
Yeah. No, a band. They were talking about supplying me, furnishing me, backing me to have a big band and rehearse with them.
Well, what did you give as your reason for not --
Well, I just didn't want it, strictly because of the fact, first of all, because I remember the situation with McShann Max Hana's band.
Yeah, I see, yeah.
And then another thing was that I was like one of the most wanted bass players in New York. In fact I had more jobs than I could stand.
Oh, yeah, probably.
And I said I would become branded as a leaders, and the guys don't want to hire a leader because they figure you're going to try to come in and run the band.
That's right. You were better off at that time --
As a side man, yeah.
Well, when do you get with Lester?
Now, Perez was across the street, and I was working with Ben. Perez was at the Spotlight, and I was with Ben.
When were you with Ben?
At the Onyx Club.
Oh, the Onyx, yes.
And we -- Perez and I would get together. He was living in the Chesterfield, and I'd walk around there

with him and we'd go have breakfast and like that, just, you know, and he kept on trying to get me to come, but I was with Ben, you know. I said, well, now he got a little bass player out of Chicago. So -- and Roy Hanes and those guys. And so I went on with Lockjaw, went up to Minton's. Then I stayed at Minton's with Ben Webster when he came in.

And that folded up, and I told Perez, why I'll go with you. I went back, went with him in '48, and Gale sent us out on tours and things, and one time we went out, we had a jacket with us. Other times Perez went out and had his eight pieces, six or eight pieces, and then we played lots of clubs in Philadelphia.

And we had Joe Jones with us then, and we got Junior Mance. Then Perez, when I was with Jazz Philharmonic, at the when he came back, I had joined with Miles Davis. And that's when we -- that's when we opened in Birdland. Opposite and Pops said Lips Page, the opening band in Birdland, you know. And then Perez comes in, and Perez wants me to stay there with him. And he brings in John Lewis and Joe Jones, a quartet, so I stayed there with him.

And then Perez went back out with Norman Granz again and Joe and I and Milt Buckner stayed there with Gene Hammonds and Sonny Stitt team. And then Joe and I became the household members. Perez and I were like -- you know, whenever Perez was back home, I was -- unless I was already

committed, I'd go back with him and work, you know, and we renewed our old tight relationship, you know, I'd wait for him. When I was working with somebody else, and he got off early, I'd wait for him and take him home all the way, you know. At first he was living down at the Mark, at a hotel down on 43rd Street.
He always talks about his cat. He called her Philharmonic. And he said something to the cat one day, and the cat didn't like it and jumped out the window.
(Laughter)
From the eighth floor. He insulted the cat. The cat jumped. So he said it hurt him so badly, but we were always tight.

Well, how did -- I mean now, we talked about, like, the rhythm sections, Basie and McShann, and we haven't said too much about Charlie Parker and bebop. Well now, how did Perez feel about the new type of rhythm sections?

Well, both he and Ben Webster were -- and Roy were, I'd say, the only people who were really vocal. Well, the other guys would say, well, man, there's something new. I ain't going to put it down, I might have to go with it. Ben Webster
That's right.
But they was vocal because, now, you'll notice that Roy and Perez and -- and Ben Webster played their solos in phrases. If a guy drops a bomb in the middle of your

phrase, it kills your phrase, you know. And so Perez would turn around to them, say, 'Just give me some tinkdee-doo,' said just like that. That's why he got rid of one drummer. And I want say were it was of a sudden -- but anyway, this gentleman was -- a guy was selling better than Perez. He was back there soloing all through Perez, you know.
So Perez would tell him, say, hey, baby, just stick to the skit, you know. Say, you know, Give me some tinkdee- boom, that's all.... Put me in the base notes. [else you'll]
(Laughter)

They -- now, Perez and the Basie band, Buster Bailey and all of them had started experimenting with what we called in Kansas City, 'running out of a key.' Now, that meant that the rhythm section stayed straight. They didn't go dropping those bombs or anything.

It was the horns that was going on. They were playing the flatted fifths and all that, stuff scales. But the rhythm section played straight, just like the Basie rhythm section or our rhythm section plays, you know. But then we came, got to New York and run across this new thing, you know, that Max and them developed, and that's really how I managed to stick in there as long as I did with all of them, Monk and Diz and all of them, because now they needed a heavy bass player, strong player to carry the beat while the drummer was the --
: The tick-pick.

Yeah, carrying on, you know, so Curly Bailey and I, we managed to just go from one -- one club to the other. whoever when we went in there, they had one of those drummers, you know, until it started to getting, you know, other a little bass players could make it. Now, there were other bass players on the streets, you know, including Pettiford, who did lots of work with those guys. Pettiford wasn't as strong in the rhythm section, but it didn't bother him what they were doing. He could walk right on through it too, you know.
And then there was John Simmons and Gaskin and Jimmy Butts wasn't too bad in there, you know.
: Well, but -- when you're saying that Ben and Lester were vocal about it, I mean they were vocal specifically, I take it, about the drums really.
Yeah, they didn't like that other -- the flatted fifths and that sort of stuff.
: Oh, I mean, well, that's --
They didn't like what was going on in the rhythm section.
: Well, no, and I mean also the -- the piano thing in the rhythm section changed too, didn't it?
Yeah, it changed, but --
: Not seriously perhaps.
No, it was changed really for the better
as far as the bass was concerned because those guys couldn't play like Basie. See, Basie could play with both hands and still stay out of the way of the bass.
Yeah.
But most of those piano players, if they used their left hand, it would be in the way of the bass player walking.
Yeah. Yeah, I see.

And so now, this new piano came up with -- he'd play a chord with his left hand, which took the place of the guitar, because by this time those guys didn't want a guitar in there. It was too much confusion in the rhythm section. So then the piano player would play the chord like the guitar player would play in his left hand, and then do his comping with the right hand.
So in a way, far as the bass player was concerned, it wasn't too bad, except the piano player looked like he was one handed, you know.
Well, that's what -- yeah, but that was primarily bad as a soloist.

Definitely, yeah. Well, I tell you another thing that happened in there at the time. First of all, remember that the guys who -- who drank whiskey could be condemned by the guys who were on the other side of the Street, who used dope, you know. And they'd come over and see you
half drunk, see Ben Webster, Perez or Hawk, somebody half drunk, and they just said, 'Man, you a drag. You're a damn drunkard.'
You mean they --
The musicians.
You don't mean the potsmokers. You mean the --
The potsmokers, yeah.
Oh, well --

And you couldn't turn around a tell a potsmoker, when he's getting too high and playing all out that he was a dope addict because now, you were squealing. You were squealing, you know. So the -- the drunks just had to take it. And Ben and Roy used to talk about this. Man, this guy's hitting me, and I can't fight back, you know.
Yeah, but what -- how would you differentiate between, we'll say, a potsmoker and a heroin addict and his attitude toward the drunks?
Well, the heroin addict --
I mean many people drank and smoked pot.
Yeah, well, it was mostly the heroin addicts that --
Well, it always seemed to me that the heroin thing became like a -- like a club or -- you know,
where the people who didn't use it were --
Were outcasts.
-- were squares.
Yeah. Yeah, that's what -- well, that's what it was. You remember when they arrested 24 guys out on -- on 52nd Street in one night?
No, I wasn't here then, no.

And that was amazing how, you know, we used to talk about it, Sid Catlett and I. We did lots of work together. And Sid and I -- well, Ben had been there, but Ben got tore up and gone about that, sit down and rest, you know. And so Sid come around there and (inaudible) that was a white rose we was hanging in at intermission, you know. He said, 'Man, isn't it amazing?' He said, 'How those federal guys knew exactly who to pick up.' He said, 'Now, we didn't want these guys down here no way because most of them weren't working, (inaudible) was just hanging down here molesting the women that come in and all that kind of stuff,' you know. And he said, 'And these cops came and picked every one of them up. There were 24 of them.'
And that was like -- part of a thing that, where I said the guys were vocal?
Yeah.
So that music that went along with it, you know, they didn't -- they were just voicing that on this
man let me -- give me a chance to be (inaudible), you know.
You know, well, you know, I remember saying to somebody once that I think the heroin in a sense changed the music too.
Yeah, it did.
Seemed to me as though the, you know, the people on that began to sort of, well, I don't know. Maybe that's a silly idea but --

No, let me -- advance, what you're saying, the way I see it from just what you said there, when those heroin smokers started coming out on the street, that ended the career for lots of trumpet players who could have played, like Cootie Williams, could have done a thing like Tricky Sam, you know. See, along with that heroin came the thing where the guy had to play a straight sound.

No tenor sax -- no saxophone player could play a growl on his horn. No trumpet player could play an imitation of a hog a grunt or nothing like that. He had to play a straight, a symphonic sound and all that, so it took away --
Well, why -- why was that? Why did they have to do that?

They put everybody down who was playing that -- who was playing the other way, Yeah, playing the other way. That's when Ben stopped doing that, because Ben was using -- used to always use a buzz until that, and he

just eased on out of it. But now when I was with Ben, he brought in Eddie Nicholson from Tulsa and -- who plays a straight, swinging drum, you know, and we had one of the best rhythm sections down on 52nd Street.
Who was that?
Eddie Nicholson. And, you know, he later got involved in that stuff with Billie Holiday.
Oh, yeah, yeah.

-- and had Dennis Thornton, who didn't have much musical knowledge, but he could comp, you know. He was no soloist, at all you know, but he could sit down in the rhythm section and play, you know, so --
Well now, when you were with -- what sort of year is it when you're with Lester Young?
Well, I'll say this. It was a happy, enjoyable year, time. See, I stayed with him off and on actually until '57.
You did?
Yeah.

Now, what was -- yes, of course, I remember when you were on records and everything with him, but what -- what was happening to him musically. I mean was he sort of -- his physical condition deteriorating and his music with it or do you think --
Well, I tell you, as he told me, you

know, he was married to a white girl. Her name was Mary. And when they put him in the service, I guess it just -- the desire to see her or something. They put him down in some Southern town. I think it was Alabama somewhere. And he sent for her.
Oh.

And he said that they used to -- they'd put him in their disciplinary barracks and, say, every night those guards would get drunk and come out there and have target practice on his head. You notice how his music, his style of music changed after he got out?
Yeah.
I think he had lots of blows on his skull, you know, and, as he said, when he got out, he made that 'DB Blues'. That was that 'Disciplinary Barracks Blues'. DB, that was like that.
What blues?
'Disciplinary Barracks Blues.'
Oh, yes, that's right.
And he named it 'DB Blues,' you know, in memory of that. But now, his --
Well, did that do serious damage, permanent damage to him?
Well, he lost coordination of his speed. He still had the feel and everything, but you see him finding
ways to shortcut and get out of holes and things with his solos and things, you know. But it didn't sound like the original Lester Young.
No. No.
And I said that he did have a bruised membrane or something in his skull. Now, you remember he and Ray Brown and Buddy Rich and I forget who played piano made that 'Up And At 'Em'?
Yeah.

This was in like someday he's going to find those soldiers, those guys that did it to him, and he was going to get right up and knock them down, you know. And then I made a record with him called 'Down And At 'Em', where he got them down there, and he -- so --
You know, the impression of this was lasting, in other words.

Yeah, he -- this was -- his phrase was nice eyes, no evil spirits. That was his favorite phrases, but he said that, but you could -- you know, he -- when we'd get off, he would mention that, you know. And then he finally met and married this colored girl named Mary too, who gave him the two kids, you know, Perez, Junior, and I can't think of the little girl's name. She's taller than I am now.
But -- and that kind of helped him to kind of pull out of it for a while. But then he started getting back on

the bottle and drank so much that he lost his taste for food, you know, and that's what actually carried him to his deterioration. In the meantime Stan Getz and all those guys would go around to his room every night and -- sometime he'd tell me, man, I say I'm going home. He said, man, he said, 'Stay here.' Maybe we can get these guys to leave, you know. They come around to his room every night to sit around and listen to his old records and have him explain to them, you know, just hung right on him, you know.
And they won an award, and he never won an award.
(Laughter)
He -- did he -- did he resent the people like Getz who were --
No. No, he kind of liked it, because everybody knew that was him.
Yeah, well, that's the proper way to look at it, although, of course, they -- the --
I think he resented Bird more than that because Leonard Feather one of the fellows had put in a book that Bird said that he was not influenced at all by -- by Prez, you know.
Bird said that?
They quoted him as saying that. But they also -- Leonard then it also quoted Bird as saying that nobody in the McShann band could play but him. And --
Nobody in the McShann band could
Well, McShann confronted him with it. He said, man, you know how these writers write. He said, you know I wouldn't say that for nothing. He said, I got my food from you all, you know.

Well, I mean this is a point, but you were saying earlier about McShann being hurt. I mean a thing is that for -- it's funny the way fate was. So, A, there was Bird, and B, there was, of all things, Walter Brown, which really was bad, wasn't it?
Yeah. Yeah.
But, yeah, but -- that's sad really. Well, then after -- after the period with Lester you were mostly sort of peaking around New York?

Yeah, well, I worked with Perez in the -- during that time when he -- when the -- when they put him in the all time hall of fame or something. That's the only award that I think that he got. We were broadcasting down at a club there across from the old Cafe Society down there. I can't remember the name of it.

And they got these things out on records. They took off Perez and I and a guy named Herb Green playing piano, Willie Jones playing drums. And that's the last time I worked with Perez. Now, I left Perez then and went with Roy and Cozy and Sal Yaged at the Metropole. I stayed over

there for two years, see.
And then I left there. I went to Europe.
: To Europe?
Yeah.
: With whom?
Buck Clayton went with me.
: Oh, yeah.

I stayed over there -- I went over there, and I stayed at the Metropole until the time to go with Buck to Europe, and when I came back from there, I went with Cootie Williams in the club that Birdland owned over there on the East Side. And we stayed over there for until about six or eight weeks. Do you remember that club? Tyree Glenn had a band upstairs.
: What was that called, the Round House?
The Roundtable, Roundtable.*
: What was you doing upstairs, the belly dancers or something?
No, we were in the main room, but Tyree and them had a -- and Arvell Shaw and Jake -- the Hanna guy, Roland Hanna and Eddie Locke were playing together with Tyree over there.
: Who were you with?
I was with Cootie Williams. He had
* The Roundtable was managed by Morris Gaxiola, who had the hotchicle concession at Birdland.
about six pieces.
Louie Williams?
Cootie -- Cootie Williams.
Cootie Williams. Oh, I'm sorry.
Oh, yeah, I remember. Yeah, that's right.

I stayed with him. Then I went out and started working with Buck doing the, you know, gigs on weekends and things, and we went back to Europe. Now, this was -- by this time it was '61, and then in '62 I went with Teddy Wilson and stayed with him until I went with Earl Hines. When I left Earl Hines, I stopped over there with Eddie Condon and stayed over there until July -- September, and I quit that and took a job in the hospital for about six months, and I got the job with Chase, you know.

But in the meantime I was still playing on weekends, you know, with Buck and different groups. I even went to (The Village Streamers) Toronto with the group that made 'Fiddler on the Roof.' It had this guy, Maranyi in it, Joe Maranyi. I went there with them.
Now, the funny thing, soon as I got in the Chase Manhattan, I got a call from Louis Armstrong wanting me to come in right away.
(Laughter)
And I said, no, probably I get in there and they'll decide to make another change and I'll have to -- because I --
Chase Manhattan, where was that,

No, I first started at 23rd and 5th. You see, when I got in Chase Manhattan, I hadn't been in there -- well, I went to school, the American Institute of Banking when I first went in, and it wasn't long before they had given me a job as -- like a teacher. And so I'd have to go, and sometimes I'd replace guys and take over for them and stay there until they could find somebody, or else I'd have to go down there and teach the new guys and that sort of thing.
Sometimes I had to go down and straighten out their books and all that sort of stuff. So I worked in -- oh, I think about 40 different Chase banks.
Oh, I didn't realize that. Yeah.
Yeah, I was over here at this one at 59th Street here and this one here at 53rd, several of them on the East side, even up as far as 79th Street on Lexington.
Now, did you -- you still played weekends, things like that, wouldn't you?

Yeah, and most of them were with Buck and Buddy. Then I went to Europe in '63. Well, I had gone to Europe. And in '69 I took off and went to -- with Jay, and we stayed over there for about a month, and I came on back to the bank, but I still was doing my things out in the -- in Hackensack, you know.
Yeah. But when -- when was it that
-- well, you must have been -- weren't you working in the same building as Vick Dickinson?
Yeah, well, that was during the time the Metropole when I was in Mexico that --
Oh, was it as far back as that? Was it? Yeah.
That's when I separated from my third wife. And I moved over there until I found a place up -- home up in the -- private home up in the what's the name of where I rented a thing, you know.
Well, what I think we ought to do now is you ought to just look through that list and see what we've missed that you want to put on.
(Recording interruption)
We've got to fill in a few details here that we bypassed about things in Kansas City.

Now, yeah, now, the Reno Club was two blocks from the Bar-le-Duc, where we were. I'll put it the other way. We were two blocks from the Reno Club, and one block, across the street and on the corner was the Green Leaf, where Bird was working with another alto player and, I think, drums and piano.
And up the street past us for about a block and a half was the Spinning Wheel, (inaudible), that was the Walden Brothers and Booker Washington, and I can't remember --
[Roselle]

Claxton and I can't remember who the other -- then Baby Love tt and -- I can't remember the name of the bass player. But now, this was an immediate circle. There was a woman named Edison that worked across the street from us that was -- further out on 12th Street there was a tap room where Roy Searcy and the guys were working, and a little further out there just before you get to the Sunset there was like an open thing, more or less like the old Metropole used to look, where Jack Parker had a group in.

And then in -- two doors or more on that same side of the street was the Lone Star, where Pete Johnson was working, and then over -- directly across from the Lone Star was the Sunset. And that was on 12th Street. Now, over on 18th Street we had the --
When you say 12th and 18th, do they run like they do in New York, I mean does 12th, 13th, 14th --
Right. Right. And so now like these were the hubs where all the activities were and --
Now, 12th and 18th, these streets run parallel?
Right.
Well, what is the street that connects them up? What would you walk up from 12th to 18th?
Well, I would advise anybody to go back two blocks to Paseo and walk --
Pasco --
-- up Paseo, which is a wide boulevard, you know.
Oh, sort of -- well, the other streets --

The other streets were very dark, alley-like streets. Now, right around about two blocks back of -- on Woodland there was a ballroom where Jimmie Lunceford played in '34, and the people were dancing and swinging so, that the floor went down about six inches. They had to cancel the dance.
Lunceford had the whole house jumping. That was some Masonic auditorium. It was an old building, you know. But they say the floor sunk about six inches.
The Masonic auditorium?
Yeah, you know.
(Laughter)

And that was on 14th Street. And now, over on 18th Street we had a Subway. Now, this is another place where we had an after hours jam session. Now, over in that area where the great Piney Brown and Felix Payne -- Felix Payne was actually the boss of all that Black neighborhood, you know. He had his connections down with whoever it was, you know.
Well, Piney Brown was what? A tavern owner?
Yeah, he ran a nightclub, but he was kind of like a man who was a friend to the musicians and, you know, and --
But I mean was he a friend of the politicians too?

Evidently he was because they probably could get him out of jail or whatever, you know. He was a big man there, and next door to his place, the Subway, was the Newt Joseph, who owned the -- he had a taxicab company, and he's the one who owned the Kansas City Monarchs. So right in that area was where all those people -- now, these were the --
Oh, the Monarchs, the baseball team?

The baseball team. And so they all hung out there now. Next door to that was what was considered as our most sophisticated hotel, was the Streets Hotel, and they had a Blue Room in there, and I don't remember the name of the band, but they had it nice, quiet. They had a beautiful dining room and very sophisticated place. It usually would fill up especially on Saturdays and Sundays and people coming by and have quiet dancing.
Now, there's Lucille's, which is right across from the Cherry Blossom and next door to the -- what's the name -- on Vine Street going towards 19th Street.
What -- which is Vine Street? Was that one parallel to Paseo?
Yes, but Vine Street was cut off by Paseo Park, which runs from 15th Street over to 17th Street.
Oh, I see.
And so Vine Street doesn't go all the way through, but it picks up again and goes on over to (inaudible) Square.
Well, Vine Street always seems to be a very important street. I mean you have 'Vine Street Boogie' and --

Well, now this is 18th and Vine and -- well, that one was 12th and Woodland, but 18th and Vine was where everybody would hang out. As I started to say, Felix Payne had an open lottery, where you go in there and gamble, you know, you bet. It was open day and night. And they had the roulette wheel and everything. It was right on the street. You could go right in there, always peace and everything.

And I would say that it was in that area where you found the hustlers. You found the good restaurants, and there was one place that's still there, and Mat law's Clothing Store, it's still there. I think it's about the only thing that's there. It's got the windows and everything barred up. Most of the buildings around there have been torn down. Mat law's is still there and --
Today, though, there isn't much life in Kansas City, is there?
Well, there's lots of --
Musical life.

It is, but it's -- it's scattered way out in the suburbs. Now, that was another thing even during our time. Kansas City wasn't directed to any one locality like, you know, the -- for instance, the Julia Lee was way out there on 60th and Truce -- yeah, 60th and Truce. And the George E. Lee was further out, At Toodie's and Tommy Douglas had a band way out. And the clubs were scattered around, but all the guys --
Were these clubs sort of in Black or white areas?
Well, the Julia Lee and those, they were in the white areas.
Oh, you know something? We haven't put anything -- there's two people I think we should just mention --that you haven't really said -- you've hardly said anything about Gus Johnson.
Yeah, well, old Gus -- Gus came from Texas too.
Oh, he did?

And he graduated from Sumner High and Sumner Junior College too. And I think he graduated from Sumner Junior -- I know he was going to Sumner Junior College. And then he left Kansas City, went up to Omaha and started to
play with some bands up there, Specs Red or somebody, and --
(End of proceedings as recorded)

Yeah, we were just saying, we were talking about drummers and which did you think were the I mean was -- you think Sonny Greer was a very -- in his peak years?
Now, Sonny -- now, there we go again. You get back comparing a small band drummer with a big band drummer. The big -- the duty of a big band drummer, he must make those dynamics with the brass.
Right.

The bass player has to play along with the reed section unless his arrangement is written so that he plays those dynamics with the brass, you know. But it's usually the thing, and this is what Gus and I, well, we just worked on, you know.

Now, with the big -- big band drummers we'd have to say that Sonny and Joe Jones were the bosses -- the original bosses, you know. And Krupa wasn't bad. Buddy Rich is good, but Buddy Rich was more or less an individualist, you know.
How about Jimmy Crawford?
Jimmy Crawford was also, with Cozy Cole. But now --
What about Shadow Wilson?
Shadow Wilson was -- well, I have to say this. Shadow Wilson came in when I was working with Basie -- they had to cut the show. They paid Gus, but they
had him lay off and had Shadow Wilson come in and play the show. Shadow was expert. He was one of my favorite drummers. In fact, I think the best bass solo I ever took was with Shadow Wilson.
Which (record inaudible) was that?
"Audubon" -- "Audubon" with Sonny Rollins on his first recording date.
Oh, yeah? And --
Now, Joe Jones and -- and -- Joe Jones and -- now, there was another drummer that was great in small band. His name was Johnson. He died -- I can't think of --
Walter Johnson?
No, Osie Walter Johnson. Yeah, Walter was good, a take-command but I wouldn't say he was (inaudible) drummer like --
No, he was like sort of a, yeah. But what about -- you haven't mentioned Sidney Catlett.

Sidney Catlett was the boss. He was the boss, and we finally started working together in '46 down on 52nd Street, and I got, oh, placards and billboards of advertisements of many jobs that we had together, you know, especially on Sunday afternoons, you know, where they had the featured All-Stars, you know, and usually Sid Catlett and I and sometimes Marlowe Morris and sometimes Sir Charles would, but Sid Catlett and I were practically on all of those.
Well, I mean when you -- he was good with
the big band and the small.

He -- he was a man that could play a thing. And there was a man -- we forgot he could play both -- a guy in Paris, lives over there now -- what's his name? Kenny Clarke -- Clarke, yeah, Klook Clarke, we call him, yeah, Kenny Clarke.

But now that thing, I still have to go back to Sonny Greer and Jo Jones, Crawford and those cats that made that rhythm section, pop, you know. They heard everything that the brass was doing. They knew how to bring the band up. You know, that first chorus, that rhythm section is not going to play that second chorus like he did that first chorus. They play that first chorus more or less and let that, especially the soloist find himself, give him a chance to relax, but that second chorus, they were supposed to blow them out of the building, you know.
And you could see --
You better just speak about when you and Gus Johnson went in Basie's band.
Well, I have a lot -- I would like to go back a little further.
Oh, all right.
Because Gus and I, before he left to go up to Omaha, I was going to Western University, and he was going to school over there at Sumner, and -- but we belonged
to the same church, and I always kid him about it. He was standing next to me, and I was singing tenor in the choir, the Trinity A.M.E. Church choir, and he was singing tenor-bass.
(Laughter)

His voice was as light as mine, but he's singing the bass line, you know. I always kid him about that. So we got together with McShann. He was having a ball. In fact, I was the only one that had a car, but in the daytime I never had my car. Gus would be over there first thing in the morning. In fact, I gave him, I had a key made so he could come and get the car.
What did he want it for?
Oh, he'd want it sometimes to take some of his people somewhere. Sometimes go out and see some chicks, whatever he wanted it for, you know --
Oh, yes.
-- I'd just let him have it, as long as he put gas in it and bring it back in time, you know.
So we kind of strayed away, after we left McShann, you know, but then I got back with him with Basie's band.
How did that come about? Who did you -- whose place did you take?
I took a young man out of -- I can't think of his name -- out of Nashville, Tennessee. And he's
doing pretty good here now. I can't think of his name, though, but he was with the septet, with the small group, and he was a good soloist and a good rhythm section, a good man, you know.

But anyway, he had trouble with one of the other members of the band. Seemed like they were going with the same girl or something. And so he quit the band. And they were out on tour with George Shearing and his group. So Al McKibbon had to double. He had to play with Basie and with the band, so they called me from Denver and asked me -- I was working the regular man in Birdland, you know. They called me at Birdland and asked me if I'd come, you know. And I said, you make the price right, I'll come.

But then when I got there, one thing I didn't realize, it was a pleasure that was that Basie working with Gus and like that, but one thing I didn't realize was that seniority I'd seen the odds then, so many guys carrying guns, you know.
(Laughter)

I thought that thing had gone out with button shoes, you know, but Gus and I, we had a good time there, and I stayed there until I found out -- they finally kept they it away from me for a long time, but I found out there was a movement to get Gus out, you know, different ones in the band. They had found a clique to get Gus out.
And that made it uncomfortable for (inaudible).
Why do you think that was? Not because of his drumming, because of a personal thing?

I don't know what it really was. I only know I'd heard that -- that he had had a couple of run-ins with different members of the band. And I don't know. It might have been that this drumming brought it on, or whatever it was, I don't know, but anyway -- and I found it out, and I just said, well, I'm not going to be any party of it, so -- Basie got me in a hotel in Detroit, and he begged me for practically all night. He brought a fifth of whiskey up there, and we talked and we talked.

I said, 'Man, I'm going; I'm leaving.' I said, you going -- I know what you going to do.' I said, 'You're going to get pressures on you, and you're going to let Gus go, and I'm not going to be here to be party of it.' And he kept Gus until Gus got sick. And Gus got sick. When he came back, he didn't have a job. Sonny Payne had it. So -- but -- Gus and I, we still remain very tight. We send each other dirty letters all the time.
Well now, one other thing that we can just get in -- veteran just say, when you quit the New York and Scene went to Texas --
Well, I retired from the bank in December, on December the 31st, 1975, but those people down at Chase Manhattan, first they didn't allow me any chance for
a promotion, although I had had a good record, got many commendations from them.
Did it have something to do with your age?
No, I think it was more due to the race.
Oh, yeah. Well --

Yeah, but anyway, so I retired on December the 31st. But now, just how -- they didn't want me to quit, and out of cruelty, they made me stay in New York until April the 2nd before I finally got my release from Chase, and I left on the 5th.
(Laughter)

And as soon as I got my release, I shipped my furniture to Texas and got in my car and tore out for Texas. I didn't even have a chance to tell guys goodbye or nothing. I was just so glad, because I was going crazy waiting for them to release me, you know.
Well, what was the property there? You -- that belonged to your people or what? You bought it somehow?
I had bought it. I bought that little farm that I had and the home (inaudible) I just applied for it, but I didn't get it until I got to Texas. So --
And so now suddenly you were a farmer?
Well, that's more or less what I'm doing.
I play with McShann, you know. We go up and do concerts and things.
Oh, you play with him.
Yeah, we go to Europe and things. We've got a lots of things booked, I think, end of this month, you know.
Where, out there?
Yeah, out West. I don't know exactly where the things -- I haven't got my contracts yet, but it pays very good money.
Oh, that's good. That's very good. Well, I don't -- you know, we can talk another hour, but there's no point in it.
Well, I would come back if you want me to. I just want to go down and meet her, since she's --
(End of proceedings as recorded)

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Born in Austin, Texas, 1913, and what the city is like
segments.summary: Ramey gives his birth date and place, and describes Austin's size, its industries, oil and cotton.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Father the teamster and the gunslinging General Hamby
segments.summary: His father, a horse trainer and farmhand, drove for the violent General Hamby, whose gun-toting habits lasted into old age.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Mother's laundry work and being the sickly youngest boy
segments.summary: His mother took in laundry and brought the children along; Ramey played on being the small, sickly baby boy.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Mother's foot organ and the songs she played
segments.summary: His mother, from a musical family, played old songs on a borrowed foot organ, such as 'Boilin' Cabbage'.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: The Glasgow family: grandmother, aunt, cousins in music
segments.summary: Mother Glasgow's restaurant, her children and the musical cousins, including Ivy who sang with Floyd Ray and later played bass.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Musical Ramey side: grandfather's violin, father's banjo, brother's quartet
segments.summary: His grandfather Jack Ramey played violin and patted his foot, as Ramey does; his father played banjo and his brother sang in a famous quartet.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Brother the prizefighter and brother-in-law Pip Sweeney
segments.summary: His oldest brother won a lightweight title before a rib injury ended it; a brother-in-law, Pip Sweeney, was a showman heavyweight.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Cousin Paris Jones, trumpeter and teacher
segments.summary: Second cousin Paris Jones taught Kenny Dorham, played jazz trumpet and stayed in Texas as a professor.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Grandmother's memory of coming from Madagascar
segments.summary: His grandmother remembered being shipped from Madagascar as a child, around the 1840s.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Boyhood chores for his grandmother and the tree-sitting business
segments.summary: He had to tend his grandmother's garden and carry her soup around town; he and his brother joked about a tree-setting business.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Grandmother's rescue story and the Glasco name
segments.summary: A family story of his grandmother being snatched from a parade, his grandfather being part Comanche, and relatives named Glasco.

segments.chapter: Childhood and family in Austin
segments.title: Father's death and the music around the cotton farm
segments.summary: His father died when Ramey was three years nine months old; relatives picked cotton together and music surrounded them.

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
segments.title: Singing at the cotton cabin, his first composition and boy preacher
segments.summary: Families sang spirituals at the cabin after picking cotton; at five Ramey made up his first song and preached.

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
segments.title: Camp meetings and the color line at church and dances
segments.summary: Holiness camp meetings drew white spectators who stood outside the tent; the same separation held at dances.

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
segments.title: Learning to sing harmony and the buck dance circle
segments.summary: He learned parts by singing between cousins, and brothers and cousins did the buck dance in a ring.

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
segments.title: Deluxe Melody Boys and George Corley's Royal Aces
segments.summary: Cousins sang with the Deluxe Melody Boys, which became George Corley's Royal Aces, where Ramey started late 1931.

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
segments.title: First instruments: timber blocks, Boy Scout drums, ukulele
segments.summary: He tried timber blocks, field drums in the Boy Scouts, a school quartet and the ukulele, and mentions Sergeant Willis.

segments.summary: Family collected records of Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith and Louis Armstrong, and sang them note for note; he recalls Blind Lemon Jefferson.

segments.chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
segments.title: From trumpet to baritone and tuba in high school
segments.summary: Air leaked from his lips on trumpet so he moved to baritone horn, then tuba, around age 11-13.

segments.title: Austin as a friendly city: Boy Scouts, lawn parties, band concerts, Mr. Timmons
segments.summary: Community activities kept Black youth busy; Friday band concerts in the park and bass horn teacher Mr. Timmons.

segments.summary: Teenage social clubs hired bands, so Ramey's Moonlight Serenaders, led by Carl Downs, formed their own dance band.

segments.summary: On 52nd Street drummers stopped carrying the beat; Ramey recalls Walter Page's lessons and New Orleans versus Chicago drumming.

segments.chapter: Bass, drums and the big-band rhythm section
segments.title: Role of the sousaphone, Eppie Jackson and the banjo
segments.summary: How the bass horn worked in early dance halls without amplification, Eppie Jackson as greatest sousaphonist, banjo cutting through.

segments.chapter: Bass, drums and the big-band rhythm section
segments.title: Why bass horns gave way and rhythm sections of the great bands
segments.summary: Bass horns were dropped as drummers toned down; rhythm sections of Ellington, Lunceford, Cab Calloway and Henderson compared.
