segments.title: Walter Page, Basie and Freddie Green: keeping out of each other's way
segments.summary: Page's balance ideas, one piano in Moten's band, Freddie Green's single chords and why bop dropped the guitar.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Leaving Austin in 1932 for Western University and working his way through
segments.summary: He left August 1932 on a music scholarship to Western University in Kansas, working odd jobs and painting buildings.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Organizing a band at Western University
segments.summary: He quickly formed a band with Buddy Anderson and Frog, buying stock arrangements like 'White Heat'.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Labor Day battle of the bands in Kansas City
segments.summary: He recalls bands like Bennie Moten, Blue Devils, Trent and George E. Lee, and a later battle against Duke Ellington.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Western band personnel and playing for Landon
segments.summary: Lawrence Anderson and Buddy Anderson were in his band and later went to McShann; they played for Landon's campaign.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Studies at Western and learning to read from Jack Washington
segments.summary: Electrical engineering, then a printing certificate; Jack Washington taught him to read music.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Switching from tuba to bass in the Western storeroom
segments.summary: He took a string bass and a saxophone from a storeroom of old band instruments, with Guy Taylor in charge.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Geography of the two Kansas Cities and the Hawaiian Gardens
segments.summary: Ramey explains Kansas City, Kansas versus Missouri and where the Hawaiian Gardens stood.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Adolphus Osborne, the bass player who quit Duke
segments.summary: A Kansas City bass player who left Duke Ellington because he disliked the harmonies and later taught in Minnesota.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Dry Kansas and wide-open Missouri; John Brown's caves
segments.summary: Musicians lived in dry Kansas and played in wide-open Missouri; Western University sat on John Brown's route.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Segregation in Missouri and Kansas schools; Reno Club
segments.summary: Kansas schools were integrated apart from Kansas City, Kansas, while Missouri clubs kept the races apart.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: The Sunset Club and meeting Prez and Ben Webster
segments.summary: The long narrow Sunset Club on 12th Street where musicians jammed until morning and Prez and Ben Webster befriended him.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Sawdust Trail, the Lone Star and Sunset crowd
segments.summary: Musicians ate breakfast at Sawdust Trail; the Lone Star with Pete Johnson and Joe Turner was classier than the Sunset.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Lester Young's and Ben Webster's styles in 1933, Dick Wilson
segments.summary: Lester's spacey tenor, Ben not yet formed, Ellington bringing it out, and Dick Wilson as local contender.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: The Cherry Blossom session where Prez cut Coleman Hawkins
segments.summary: Lester Young outplayed Hawkins at a jam session, then was fired by Fletcher Henderson for his tone.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Lester Young as a big brother
segments.summary: Lester was kind to Ramey, who gave him his tenor saxophone, and he took up with Countess Johnson.

segments.chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
segments.title: Countess Johnson and other women pianists
segments.summary: Countess Johnson replaced Mary Lou Williams with Kirk, died young; another woman pianist played across the street.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Oliver Todd's high school band and the start of Countess Johnson's band
segments.summary: Oliver Todd's band was taken over by Charlie Green, so five members formed a band with Countess Johnson on 12th Street.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Personnel of the Countess Johnson group: Piggy Minor, Earl Jackson, Bill Nolan
segments.summary: Piggy Minor, Earl Jackson, William Scott and Bill Nolan, several of whom went to McShann; Earl Jackson versus John Jackson.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Clubs the Countess band played: Bar la Duc, Movie Chateau, State Line Tavern
segments.summary: They broadcast nightly and played clubs whose tunes they carried over to McShann.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Day job as assistant engineer at Western while playing nights
segments.summary: Married with a child, he took a $45-60 a month job at Western and played 8-to-4 clubs, napping in the boiler room.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Countess Johnson's piano style
segments.summary: Her style fell between Earl Hines and Basie, fast and effortless; she never sang.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Earl Hines on the radio and listening in Texas
segments.summary: In 1928-29 Texas musicians listened on the radio to Earl Hines, Herman Waldman and Alphonso Trent.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Trent's band and how Basie's band built a following by socializing
segments.summary: Alphonso Trent was a good band; Basie's men mixed with ordinary people, pimps and prostitutes, which advertised them, unlike Andy Kirk's.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Earl Hines's influence everywhere, stretched tenths
segments.summary: Hines was the biggest piano influence after the barrelhouse players; rumour said his webs were cut to stretch tenths. Includes a hotel interruption.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Countess Johnson's later years and a possible Billie Holiday record
segments.summary: She left to replace Mary Lou with Kirk, died soon after; Ramey believes she recorded with Billie Holiday.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Her brother Roy Johnson, pianist and later Hampton's bassist
segments.summary: Roy Johnson played piano in Kansas City and later bass with Lionel Hampton.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Everett Johnson, barrelhouse pianist
segments.summary: Everett Johnson battled Pete Johnson all night and was for a time more popular.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Why Basie got publicity and Andy Kirk did not
segments.summary: Basie had Benny Goodman and John Hammond behind him, while Kirk lacked backers though he was most popular in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: Riffs versus orchestration: Basie's reeds and Harlan Leonard
segments.summary: Basie's band relied on riffs backing soloists, whereas Harlan Leonard's was over-arranged and McShann's men outblew them.

segments.chapter: Countess Johnson's band and the Kansas City scene
segments.title: After Countess Johnson: a Flint bandleader's band and a walkathon job
segments.summary: Before joining McShann in April 1938, Ramey worked for a Flint, Michigan leader and the walkathon band.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Tape change
segments.summary: Brief break and talk about what to cover next.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Walter Brown's nasal singing compared with Jay McShann and Sinatra
segments.summary: They discuss Walter Brown's diction and Jay McShann's singing; Ramey admires singers who state the melody as written.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Side change and picking up the thread
segments.summary: Side one begins; Ramey recalls where they were after Countess Johnson.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: The walkathon band at the Playmore Ballroom
segments.summary: A four- or five-piece black band played a walkathon at a hall that had admitted only white bands.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Walkathons as an offshoot of medicine-show band work
segments.summary: Walkathons followed carnival and medicine-show tent bands, with the band playing for contestants indoors.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: The Cherry Blossom and Vine Street's musicians' hotels and clubs
segments.summary: The Cherry Blossom was the old Eblon Theatre where Basie once played organ; the street had the Booker T. Washington Hotel and Kentucky Tavern.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Spook breakfasts and McShann's nickname Hootie
segments.summary: Spook breakfasts were all-night jam sessions; 'spook' meant ghost, and Jay McShann was Hootie for staying up like an owl.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Playing with Bus Moten's group and the union threat
segments.summary: After the walkathon he worked briefly with Bus Moten's group and was threatened by the union to join in 1934.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Where Benny Moten's band worked
segments.summary: Moten played parks like Fairyland and Winwood Beach and bands booked themselves.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Kansas City bands touring Texas and raiding local musicians; Earl Hines
segments.summary: Bands came to Texas regularly and took musicians back; Hines was known for stealing players, including from McShann.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Bus Moten's piano and accordion playing
segments.summary: Ramey found Bus Moten a soloist who went off on his own chords, easier on accordion.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Benny Moten as organizer, Blanche Calloway and the Missourians
segments.summary: Benny Moten was a modest pianist but a good manager; talk of Blanche and Cab Calloway's Missourians.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Bus Moten's eight-piece band, the Reno Club scramble and the Continental
segments.summary: Several bands tried to get the Reno Club after Basie left; Dee Stewart and the Continental near the Muehlebach.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: What Walter Page taught about restraint and supporting the soloist
segments.summary: Ramey met Page in 1932; Page taught him to play a straight line, move opposite the melody, and not show up other players.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Learning bass from a Frank Skinner chart
segments.summary: He taught himself using a chart pasted on his bass, despite his double-jointed fingers.

segments.chapter: Walkathons, Moten and Walter Page
segments.title: Double-jointed fingers as a handicap
segments.summary: They examine how his fingers bend, hurting speed, endurance and bowing.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Oliver Todd's job at Smith's Tavern and the drummer who was beaten
segments.summary: The Christmas 1937 job at Smith's Tavern, drummer Bobby Stafford beaten for leaving, Todd as second trumpet.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Meeting Jay McShann at the Taproom and spook breakfasts
segments.summary: Ramey met Jay at jam sessions at the 12th Street Taproom; McShann's rhythm section was Jesse Price and Billy Hadnott.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Opening at Martin's on the Plaza: Gus Johnson and Pete McShann
segments.summary: Pete McShann drummed for two weeks until Gus Johnson came from Omaha; Pete was Jay's cousin.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann's age and personality
segments.summary: Ramey, three years older, was the oldest in the band; Jay looked young, friendly, now more business-like.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann's money: royalties, garbage trucks and investments
segments.summary: Dance and Ramey discuss how McShann made money, including garbage trucks and royalties.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Becoming close friends with McShann, who drank
segments.summary: Ramey kept the job and they became close friends while McShann was drinking heavily.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Reel III header
segments.summary: Smithsonian Reel III header noting McShann.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann's seven-piece opening group and the local's zoning objection
segments.summary: Seven pieces opened including Bob Mabane, a baritone and singer Joe Williams; the white local claimed they were out of territory.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Martin's on the Plaza: the restaurant and its schedule
segments.summary: The Plaza was an elite area; the band played soft music then dance music, 20 minutes on and 40 off.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Drinking on the job and a drummer's habits
segments.summary: The band rarely drank on the job; Ramey tells about a drummer drunk afternoons and nights and his marriage.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Chicken in the basket song and Vine Street Varieties
segments.summary: Ramey's jingle on 'Pennies from Heaven', the Saturday show at the Lincoln Theater and Dave Dexter's fondness for McShann.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann as pianist and the band's ballad repertoire
segments.summary: McShann was loved as a pianist; at Martin's they played pop tunes more than hot ones.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann's later study and piano style
segments.summary: Dance asks if McShann's conservatory study and Tatum changed his playing; Ramey notes the difference between solo and band pianists.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: The happy McShann band and 'The Master's in His Solitude'
segments.summary: McShann created a family atmosphere and a half-finished tune that gave rise to the flatted fifth.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann underrated; Earl Hines the same
segments.summary: McShann is introduced only as Parker's discoverer, and Hines too is asked mainly about others.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Hines and McShann treated as footnotes to Armstrong and Parker; Michael's Pub
segments.summary: Both are asked mainly about others; Dance describes McShann being buried at Newport and helping him at Michael's Pub.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: McShann played down on the Charlie Parker package tour
segments.summary: McShann was hurt when a tour presented a Parker authority as the star; Dance says George Wein's package flopped in Berlin.

segments.chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
segments.title: Ramey threatens to quit McShann's European tour over a loud fiddler
segments.summary: A fiddle-playing guest dominated the group on the Europe trip; Ramey objected, and talks about McShann's temper.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Martin's and the Continental, and Charlie Barnet's offer hidden from Ramey
segments.summary: Three months at Martin's, then switching with the Continental; McShann and Tumino concealed Barnet's offer.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Wichita, the Down Beat poll and the Chicago trip
segments.summary: McShann built a base in Wichita; Down Beat voted them promising and he and Jay were brought to Chicago for six weeks.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Front-line changes and Bird's comings and goings
segments.summary: Earl Jackson, Piggy, Scotty and Bird swapped places in the band; Bird hoboed to New York and Lester came from Ernie Fields.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: John Tumino, the Century Room, the big band and Don Robey's tours
segments.summary: Tumino co-owned and booked the band, leased the Century Room, bought uniforms; Don Robey booked tours in Texas.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Assembling the big band
segments.summary: Ramey and McShann went to Omaha to fetch Bob Merrill; others came from Towles and Ernie Fields.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Parker's arrangement 'What Price Love' and the Dallas Decca session
segments.summary: Ramey remembers only one Parker arrangement, recorded in Dallas, which Decca rejected for blues.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Walter Brown's background and flat blues singing
segments.summary: Walter Brown came from a CCC camp near Topeka; Dance finds his singing deadpan.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Reel 4 header and index
segments.summary: Smithsonian Reel 4 header (Washington, September 1978) with topic index.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Walter Brown and the blues singers of Kansas City
segments.summary: Brown was a stranger to the band; local blues singers imitated Rushing and Turner, and McShann had used ballad singers.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: How 'Confessin' the Blues' and 'Jumpin' the Blues' were made up
segments.summary: The head arrangements for the 1941-42 records were worked out orally, Ramey wrote eight bars and Bird four, building from an old blues theme.

segments.chapter: Building McShann's big band and blues records
segments.title: Charlie Parker before and after George E. Lee: 'Lady Be Good'
segments.summary: Ramey knew Bird from 1934 as a poor player; he returned in 1937 playing Lester Young's solo note for note.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Lester Young's influence on Bird and Buster Smith's role
segments.summary: Armstrong influenced Lester, Lester influenced Bird, and Buster Smith made the Basie band.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Buster Smith's riffs at spook breakfast jam sessions
segments.summary: Buster set tricky riffs that other horns had to harmonize, eliminating anyone who missed, which taught Bird.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Buster Smith as alto and clarinet soloist
segments.summary: Buster had a soft alto sound, and outplayed Benny Goodman on clarinet.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Why Buster Smith faded; finding the Blue Devils survivors
segments.summary: Buster was easy-going, lives in Dallas and plays piano; he is one of few Blue Devils left and regrets not joining Basie.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: An outside interviewer who paid fifty dollars
segments.summary: Ramey recounts a university researcher who interviewed him, paid him fifty dollars and was slow to send tapes.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Riff bands and head arrangements: Buster Smith made the Basie band
segments.summary: The Basie and McShann bands were made by head arrangements, with reed and brass riffs, and the best often are blues.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Blues hits and Kansas City jazz as revival meeting
segments.summary: Dance cites hit blues by Ellington; Ramey says Kansas City jazz imitates camp meeting revivals.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: What was specifically Kansas City: riffs, looseness and playing behind the beat
segments.summary: Dance and Ramey debate whether riffs were a Kansas City invention; McShann played behind the beat, as on 'Hootie Blues'.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Eastern metronomic beat versus Western backbeat and the churchy rhythm section
segments.summary: Eastern rhythm sections kept a metronome beat, while Kansas City and Ellington rhythm sections accented, rooted in church.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Cozy Cole and ageing drummers' legs
segments.summary: They discuss Cozy Cole's change in style and how older drummers tire in the foot.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Lunceford, Claude Hopkins and McKinney's Cotton Pickers rhythm sections
segments.summary: Lunceford's section had a churchy feel; Hopkins and McKinney's Cotton Pickers also swung.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Hearing Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Ramey heard Henderson only once or twice and was biased toward Kansas City bands.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Looseness of Kansas City bands; Columbia's Lester Young reissues and John Hammond
segments.summary: Dance objects that reissues of Basie records are issued under Lester Young's name, thanks to Hammond.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Prez, John Hammond and Prez's firing from Basie
segments.summary: Ramey, who worked with Prez at Birdland, tells why Prez resented Hammond, who got him and Billie Holiday out of Basie's band.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Basie personnel changes: Claude Williams, Tabby Smith, Joe Keyes
segments.summary: Why certain players left Basie's band, from temper and lip trouble to alcoholism and thin lead tone.

segments.chapter: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
segments.title: Ellington's and Basie's powerful rhythm sections
segments.summary: Basie's rhythm section held the looser band together; Ellington's with Braud and Greer was amazing, heard on 'Ring Them Bells'.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Rhythm sections leave the heavy bass drum behind; Hines brings the piano forward
segments.summary: Sonny Greer teamed with the bass fiddle, 1928 Luis Russell records show the shift, and Earl Hines made the solo pianist heard in a big band.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: How the McShann rhythm section found each other; the guitar player
segments.summary: Influenced by Basie and above all Page, Ramey, McShann and Gus Johnson let the rhythm section walk alone; a guitarist was added in 1941.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: 'Swingmatism' and the stolen band book
segments.summary: Only one band arrangement, Scotty's 'Swingmatism', was recorded; McShann's book was later stolen.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Leading the band on tour in 1944: Bird and a bandmate beaten by Mississippi police
segments.summary: On the way to California with McShann gone, police at Natchez beat Bird and another man; Ramey recalls Bird talking them out of trouble elsewhere.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: McShann's induction and the Amarillo dance
segments.summary: McShann played one night at the Plantation Club before the Army; Ramey took the band back, giving their own dance in Amarillo.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Pianists Bob Merrill and Skip Hall
segments.summary: Bob Merrill filled in at piano and Skip Hall travelled as arranger before entering service.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Refusing to front the band under Walter Brown's name
segments.summary: Ramey was promised direction of the band, but management renamed it Walter Brown's, so he refused and left.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: The stolen music, Lucky Enois and the earlier lost trunk
segments.summary: The band's music was stolen from the auditorium; Ramey recalls a previous loss in Baltimore blamed on Lucky Enois.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Ramey's scrapbook and John Tumino's sacrifices
segments.summary: Ramey gave his scrapbook and telegram to Tumino and never got them back; Tumino went without for the band.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Opening at the Savoy against Lucky Millinder, February 1942
segments.summary: Millinder's postcard threatened to send them back to the sticks; after a hard Pennsylvania drive they opened on the Sultans' bandstand.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: The band's shabby uniforms and non-stop playing
segments.summary: They had one uniform, cardboard stands and pinned-on derbies, and sweated through every set.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: Millinder's band heated up and how Joe Glaser paid
segments.summary: Millinder's band was strong; he jumped on the piano; of Glaser's bands Millinder paid best.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: The 'Roll 'Em' story and Lucky's constant firings
segments.summary: Dance relays that Lucky sat in after McShann played a blues thirty minutes; Millinder always changed men.

segments.chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
segments.title: The Sunday 'Cherokee' broadcast
segments.summary: On their first Sunday matinee Bird and the rhythm section played 'Cherokee' for 45 minutes over the radio and musicians crowded the stand.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Reel 5 header
segments.summary: Smithsonian Reel 5 header with topics Parker, drug scene, Prez, Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Parker's triumph in New York and his unnoticed visit in 1939
segments.summary: Dance and Ramey credit the McShann band and Parker for the Savoy impact; in 1939 Bird played New York for $6 a night and was ignored.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Bird fired for the fight with Walter Brown and then rehired
segments.summary: After Bird and Brown's slow-motion fight, Ben Bart demanded he be fired; Ramey became his agent and got him back.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Southern tour: promoters running off with the money
segments.summary: In Augusta and Virginia, promoters vanished with receipts and the band paid out of pocket to avoid jail.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Personnel changes: Jimmy Forrest, Paul Quinichette and Bird
segments.summary: Players quit in Kansas City; they added Jimmy Forrest and Paul Quinichette, and Walter Brown and Paul got arrested in San Antonio.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Singers Hibler, Bill Nolan and Walter Brown
segments.summary: Nolan sang ballads before Brown; Al Hibbler joined in San Antonio; Witherspoon came after Ramey left.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Bird leaves for Earl Hines and buys Ramey a coat
segments.summary: Bird left McShann in fall 1942, joined Hines, and bought Ramey a second-hand coat.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Leaving the band after a knife fight with Bob Merrill
segments.summary: In Boston, Merrill came at Ramey over torn music and Ramey cut him, so he quit and took packing-house work.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: The danger of carrying a knife
segments.summary: Dance and Ramey agree a weapon tempts use; Dance recalls Tizol and Cat Anderson.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Resentment in the band over Ramey's featured role
segments.summary: Because of the Barnet citation, Ramey was shown off with visiting bands, and band members resented him.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Giving up bass solos after beating Oscar Pettiford
segments.summary: Ramey out-played Pettiford at the Spotlight, then stopped soloing at Birdland to avoid trouble.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Opinions on bass solos and bands
segments.summary: Ramey and Dance agree bass solos are overdone; Walter Page took none.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Returning to McShann and the pitcher incident
segments.summary: McShann called him back; the cops dropped it since Ramey was nearly hit with a pitcher.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: The band collapses after McShann is drafted
segments.summary: When Ramey refused the Brown plan, the band folded; Gus Johnson entered service in November 1943.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Bird's addiction, nutmeg and benzedrine
segments.summary: Bird stayed in control while followers copied him; he introduced nutmeg and soaked reeds in benzedrine water. Ramey never took drugs.

segments.chapter: Bird, the band's breakup and Luis Russell
segments.title: Working the Reno Club and joining Luis Russell's band
segments.summary: After McShann, he worked six weeks at the new Reno with Todd and joined Luis Russell with Lil Green when their bassist left.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Luis Russell's weak band with Lil Green, Gatemouth Moore and the Ink Spots
segments.summary: Russell's band had few real soloists but backed Lil Green and Gatemouth Moore on packages from Moe Gale's office.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: The Howard Callender band photograph
segments.summary: Dance shows a photo of a band under Howard Callender; Ramey is unsure whether he was in it and calls them marching-band musicians.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Settling in New York: Lips Page and the Local 802 probation
segments.summary: Lips Page got him work on 52nd Street while the union barred him from out-of-town bands for six months.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: McShann out of the Army, Ben Webster and Tiny Grimes
segments.summary: Barry Ulanov pressed him to return to McShann but Ramey explained the union rule, then worked with Ben Webster and Tiny Grimes.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Declining Teddy Reig's offer of a big band in 1949
segments.summary: He turned down backing for a big band, remembering McShann's band and wanting to stay a sideman.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Working with Lester Young: Birdland and the cat named Philharmonic
segments.summary: Ramey worked with Ben Webster at the Onyx, then with Prez from 1948 at Birdland, remaining close.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Prez, Ben Webster and Roy Eldridge on bebop drumming; why Ramey stayed in demand
segments.summary: Older players disliked drummers dropping bombs; Ramey and Curly Russell survived with a strong beat.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: How the piano comping changed with bebop
segments.summary: The new pianists played chords in the left hand in place of the guitar, which suited the bassist.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Drinkers against dope users and the 52nd Street arrests
segments.summary: Drug users condemned drinkers as drunks; Ramey and Sid Catlett recall the roundup of twenty-four on 52nd Street.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Heroin and the straight sound; Ben Webster's rhythm section
segments.summary: Heroin-era players abandoned growls and effects; Ben Webster dropped his buzz, and his rhythm section was one of 52nd Street's best.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Lester Young's army abuse and its effect on his playing
segments.summary: Prez told Ramey that guards used his head for target practice in the disciplinary barracks, which changed his style and led to 'D.B. Blues'.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Prez's decline and Stan Getz
segments.summary: Prez's drinking cost him his appetite; younger saxophonists like Stan Getz hung around his room.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Bird's misquotation about Prez and McShann
segments.summary: A writer quoted Bird denying Lester's influence and saying no one in McShann's band could play; Bird denied it to McShann.

segments.chapter: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
segments.title: Last work with Prez and the Metropole
segments.summary: Ramey's last job with Prez was a broadcast; he then joined Roy Eldridge, Cozy Cole and Sal Yaged at the Metropole for two years.

segments.chapter: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited
segments.title: Europe with Buck Clayton, Cootie Williams, Teddy Wilson and Earl Hines
segments.summary: After the Metropole he went to Europe with Buck Clayton, then Cootie Williams, Teddy Wilson, Hines and Eddie Condon.

segments.chapter: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited
segments.title: Working at Chase Manhattan Bank while playing weekends
segments.summary: Ramey worked about forty Chase branches and taught banking, played weekends with Buck Clayton, and toured with Jay in 1969.

segments.chapter: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited
segments.title: Clubs along 12th Street in Kansas City
segments.summary: Ramey maps the Reno, Bar-le-Duc, Green Leaf, Spinning Wheel, Lone Star and Sunset, and how to walk between 12th and 18th.

segments.chapter: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited
segments.title: Lunceford's sinking floor, 18th and Vine, Piney Brown and Felix Payne
segments.summary: The Masonic hall floor sank when Lunceford played; around 18th and Vine were the Subway, Newt Joseph, Streets Hotel, Lucille's and Felix Payne's lottery.

segments.chapter: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited
segments.title: Kansas City clubs scattered in the suburbs
segments.summary: Even in his time Julia Lee, George E. Lee and Tommy Douglas played far-flung clubs, many in white areas.

segments.chapter: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited
segments.title: Gus Johnson's Texas and Kansas City background
segments.summary: Gus came from Texas, attended Sumner High and Junior College, then went to Omaha.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Reel 6 header
segments.summary: Smithsonian Reel 6 header.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Big band drummers: Sonny Greer, Jo Jones, Shadow Wilson
segments.summary: Ramey compares small and big-band drummers; Shadow Wilson subbed for Gus Johnson in Basie's band and played on 'Audubon'.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Sid Catlett, Kenny Clarke and how a rhythm section builds choruses
segments.summary: Sid Catlett was the boss; Ramey worked with him from 1946 and explains the second-chorus lift.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Gus Johnson in the church choir and borrowing Ramey's car
segments.summary: Ramey and Gus sang in the Trinity A.M.E. choir before McShann, and Gus used his car.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Joining Basie's band alongside Gus and leaving over the clique against Gus
segments.summary: Ramey replaced a bassist at Basie's request, found a clique to oust Gus, and left after Basie begged him in Detroit.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Retiring from Chase Manhattan, denied promotion because of race
segments.summary: He retired December 1975 after being denied promotion, which he attributes to race.

segments.chapter: Drummers, Basie's band and retirement
segments.title: Moving to the Texas farm and playing with McShann; close of interview
segments.summary: He left New York in April 1976 for Texas, farms and still plays concerts with McShann.
